items.body: With Sounds From The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System, Bios Contrast & Nilotpal Das abruptly change course from the expansive drone works of Meltwater Pulse (2023) and Dragon Rising (2022). The album arrives in violent bursts, assembled from Bangla rap, digital hardcore, dek bass, ambient electronics, and an unusually large network of collaborators stretching from Kolkata to Europe and East Asia. Its premise—a world descending into collective psychosis during the Kali Yuga, inspired in part by Das’s own experience of Schizophrenia Spectrum Disorder—could easily have become an exercise in conceptual excess. Instead, organised chaos is built into the record itself. The constant collision of genres, collaborators, and production techniques refuses to settle into a single musical language. From the opening “Schizophrenic Intro”, the listener is thrown into a vortex of slowed-down, sped-up, looped, reversed, and glitched material, with no attempt to ease the transition. The abrasive momentum of “Gondho Jhaater Chule” barely relents in “Escape”, whose spectral vocals provide only the briefest moment of respite before “Iron Age Fantasies” introduces melodic gestures recalling classic Tollywood soundtracks, immediately distorting them into something deeply uncanny. “Laurar Baal” and “Laura Chos” push the collision between noise, Bengali rap, and sampled film dialogue to breaking point, while “E.M.P.” suspends the album inside an extended electronic blackout, one of its most absorbing passages. The unexpected arrival of the Korean gayageum and daegeum (the former a traditional twelve-string plucked zither with a wooden resonating chamber, the latter a large transverse bamboo flute known for its resonant, buzzing tone) on “Cappucc1n0” offers neither resolution nor sentimentality, but a fragile interruption before “Radio Paranoia” and “Maniac Outro” complete the descent into sonic disintegration. The use of crude sexual slang and bodily imagery—particularly in “Gondho Jhaater Chule”, “Laurar Baal”, and “Laura Chos”—adds another layer of instability, grounding the album’s apocalyptic vision in the language of the street as much as in mythology. Vulgarity and transcendence coexist throughout the record, collapsing distinctions between the sacred and the profane with the same ease that it moves between Bangla bass, digital hardcore, ambient electronics, and noise. The density of the album can feel overwhelming at times, and it continually rewires expectations. Yet every stylistic shift destabilises the previous one without feeling arbitrary, reflecting Das’s conception of schizophrenia not as a metaphor but as a lived condition in which disparate realities coexist simultaneously. The album’s many collaborators are given considerable freedom, yet the result never fragments into disconnected contributions; instead, their contrasting vocabularies reinforce the instability at the heart of the project. Challenging but consistently rewarding, Sounds From The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System places the listener inside the eye of its own sonic vortex, where overload becomes its organising principle rather than an obstacle to it. Corresponding via email, Nilotpal Das sheds further light on the production process. photo by @roh4nlifts at Chandraketugarh Your earlier releases as Bios Contrast—from Dragon Rising and Meltwater Pulse to the forthcoming twelve-hour harmonium drone project under your own name—often revolved around expansive historical, geological, or spiritual concepts explored through long-form composition. Sounds From The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System, by contrast, is fragmented, densely collaborative, and rooted in digital hardcore, Bangla rap, experimental electronics, and what you describe as “Brahmancore.” What drew you toward this radically different format? Do you see the album as a departure from your earlier practice, or simply another way of pursuing the same fascination with large-scale conceptual worlds? Sounds From The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System is a very personal album. At the same time, it is a pursuit of a large-scale conceptual world. I wouldn’t say the theme of the album is conceptual, but rather very real. I suffer from Schizophrenia Spectrum Disorder, so it’s a take on my worldview. Everything is random and unnecessary but, at the same time, needed, just like the world we live in. People would call me crazy, but I really felt the presence of something godlike, something that controls all of us humans. The album imagines a world descending into mass psychosis during the Kali Yuga, with schizophrenia functioning as both narrative device and sonic metaphor. At the same time, it brings together artists from very different musical and geographical backgrounds—BROOD, Kush Arora, Kim Hae Kyung, Ellery Everet, Seraphim, enesai, P.U.S.Y.E.T.E.R., and many others. How did you coordinate such a diverse group of collaborators while maintaining a coherent dramatic arc? Did each artist respond to a specific chapter in the narrative, or were they encouraged to reinterpret the concept through their own musical language? I didn’t make this album to express or present a very linear story. Every collaborator was free to interpret the concept in their own way. The record is schizophrenic in the sense that it collages many different sounds and genres while maintaining its central theme, which is chaos. And chaos happens naturally while collaborating. At first, I put out an open call for collaborators on Instagram. Many artists quickly DM’d me, and we started a group where we exchanged stems and sounds. Throughout your work you’ve often spoken about “curating sounds” rather than creating something entirely new, drawing on traditional instruments, field recordings, sampling, improvisation, and careful research. On Sounds From The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System, that curatorial approach seems to expand into an entire network of voices, genres, and production methods, from Bangla rap and digital hardcore to ambient passages and Korean traditional instruments. Did working with so many collaborators change your understanding of authorship? At what point does a project of this scale stop feeling like an individual album and become a collective sound world? I started this project with the intention of creating the most mainstream, non-experimental trash music imaginable. The result, however, is the most experimental music I’ve worked on so far. I wasn’t controlling the direction the project was taking; it was a collaborative effort, and it still is. Sounds From The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System is also the result of a video game that Kim Hae Kyung is currently developing, called The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System. In an earlier interview you described Kolkata as having only a small experimental music community, while also expressing admiration for artists working across South Asia. Since then, you’ve collaborated with musicians from Europe, North America, East Asia, and beyond, building an unusually international artistic network. Has making Sounds From The S.P.E.A.K.E.R. System changed your perspective on where your music belongs? Do you feel part of a global experimental community now, and how has continuing to work from Kolkata shaped the way you approach collaboration and the exchange of ideas? I would say I don’t belong to an experimental community anymore, but rather to a community that spans many genres, so I fit in with everyone. I like all kinds of music. Kolkata has always had a small experimental community, so I’ve simply accepted that and moved on to other communities. I like mainstream, hard-hitting music now—if the music goes hard, I’m all in, regardless of genre. I have a lot of connections with international artists, and I feel I belong to a global community rather than just a local one, because collaborating is fun, and collaborating with people who have totally different ideas and perspectives is even more fun. (Gianmarco Del Re)
items._genre: experimental electronic / Bangla rap / digital hardcore / ambient noise / world fusion
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑从Bios Contrast与Nilotpal Das此前的氛围drone作品中急转弯，以暴烈的碎片化拼贴构建关于卡利时代集体精神崩溃的声音叙事。Bangla说唱、digital hardcore、dek bass、ambient electronics等异质元素被强行碰撞，素材不断被减速、加速、循环、反向、glitch化处理，从开篇便将听者抛入失序漩涡。多位来自加尔各答至欧洲、东亚的合作者被赋予高度自由，作品却并未因此分崩离析，而是以schizophrenia作为结构逻辑——异质现实的同时共存。专辑中可听到被扭曲的Tollywood旋律、街头粗俗俚语与神话意象的并置，以及韩国伽倻琴与大笒的突然闯入，不提供任何和解性的解决，只留下一连串不稳定的断裂。整体密度极具压迫感，但每一次风格转向都在拆解前一个设定，构成一张密度极高且听觉逻辑严密的实验作品。

items.body:
STROOM fills in a gap on the timeline, excavating vital experiments made in Cologne in the wake of the cult 'Novaya Scena' compilation by Svitlana Nianio, Michael Springer, Guido Erfen, Soloveyka, Yewgeny Taran and Wolfram Burgtorf.

Back in 1993, a bizarre 20-track compilation appeared from Cologne's musical fringe. The idea for the set had come from artist and producer Erfen and sound engineer and percussionist Springer, two close friends who, taking advantage of cheap rent and disused buildings, put on regular events and established a recording studio in their neighborhood, off the beaten track. Erfen was a dedicated tape trader and had received a transmission from Kharkiv's Novaya Scena rock club that arrived with an essay and music from three local bands. At this time, Ukraine was still under Soviet rule and the music fascinated the two friends, shining a spotlight on a part of the world they were completely unfamiliar with. When singer and keyboardist Soloveyka visited cologne a year later, she handed Erfan more tantalizing music, inspiring him to make his own pilgrimage to Ukraine to investigate further. The research resulted in the 'Novaya Scene' CD, a set of tracks recorded between 1986 and 1992 that muddled prog with new wave, punk, folk and avant-garde rock. It was released on Hamburg's What's So Funny About label and was supposed to have a sequel.

That's where 'Aftermath and Transitions' comes in. Following the release of 'Novaya Scena', Erfen and Springer set up a series of sessions at their studio, inviting some of the Ukrainian artists to record with them. It's this period that resulted in Svitlana Nianio's 'Transilvania Smile' soundtrack that was properly released for the first time on Muscat sublabel Shukai in 2023. Nianio had been a member of Cukor Bila Smerť (the band who'd provided the stylistic anchor for 'Novaya Scena') and took the opportunity to launch her solo career, with Springer working as engineer. And there was more material from those sessions that Springer held back: the compilation's first four tracks are collaborations between Nianio, Springer, Taran and Springer's good friend Burgtorf. Opener 'Fake' was almost finished when Nianio showed up at the studio with her Casio in tow, so Springer plugged her in and she ended up lavishing the beat with vocals in Ukrainian and oddball keyboard vamps. The other three tracks were a little more organic, improvised in the studio while the artists got familiar with one another - there's the decelerated reggae experiment 'ManySpace', the instrumental groover 'Quiet Place' and best of all 'Політ Світляки', a wiry percussive jam that's not aged a day.

Erfen joins in on the ace exotica-tinged 'Whispering Walls' and 'Tired River', tracks from the group's final session in 1995. Nianio and Taran were planning to renew their visas and return to Cologne to record more, but it never happened - the recordings were shelved and the artists went about their lives independently. Then there's the three Solar tracks recorded by Soloveyka and Burgtorf who struck up a friendship after meeting at Springer's studio. Singing in Russian and English, Soloveyka breathes cabaret energy over Burgtorf's jerky, sample-heavy ethno-groove productions. And it's left to Taran to finish things off, with a "1996 Version" of his 'Death and the Bachelor' track that features none other than Nianio on keys. Phew. It's a brilliant set, really - not just one for STROOM obsessives, it'll speak to anyone whose interest in the Ukrainian underground was piqued by 'Transilvania Smile' or Muscut's ace Cukor Bila Smerť anthology.
items._genre: experimental / avant-garde / post-punk / world fusion / lo-fi
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑记录了1994至1996年间科隆地下音乐人与乌克兰艺术家合作的实验结晶。缘起于制作人Erfe与录音师Springer在1993年偶然收到来自哈尔科夫Novaya Scena摇滚俱乐部的磁带，由此展开对乌克兰独立音乐场景的深入挖掘。前四首曲目由Nianio、Springer、Taran与Burgtorf在工作室中即兴创作完成，融合了减速雷鬼实验、器律动与尖锐打击乐质感。此外收录了Erfe参与的异域风格曲目'Whispering Walls'与'Tired River'，源自1995年最终一次录音session。Nianio原本计划续签签证返回科隆继续合作，但最终未能实现，这些素材被搁置多年。合辑展现了东欧前卫摇滚、新浪潮与西方实验即兴美学的罕见交汇。

items.body:
Topdown Dialectic’s solo debut bow on False Aralia rounds up over a decade of material in supremely elusive style & pattern - all rug-pulling rhythms and hallucinatory fractals wrapped up with proper, hyperreal frisson. Massive chef’s kiss FFO Vladislav Delay, Beatrice Dillon, Paperclip Minimiser, Purelink, Marc Leclair.

An artist keenly observed since initial gestures on /\\Aught in the early ‘10s, and throughout their cult LP trilogy for Peak Oil during 2018-2021; Topdown Dialectic has become a unique facet of C.21st dub electronics, adored for their grasp of diffused spatio-textural sorcery and wraithlike grooves. Anyone paying close attention to emergent sounds via Peak Oil and its False Aralia offshoot may have guessed at TD’s signature, watermarked imprint on the Borgesian Term EP of late ’25, which can now be confirmed as the work of one and the same Izaak Schlossmann; a photographer and producer patently in possession of heightened proprioceptions and a rewardingly patient approach to lushly dissociative sonification. In other words, he makes some of the sexiest electronic music out there - stuff that genuinely feels like it was made this century - and his latest practically leaves you kissing the sky thru its 80 minutes of lip-biting, skin tingling pressure. 

On 16 tracks timed at exactly 5 minutes each, we’re placed in the presence of suggestive sorcery, eliding unarchived material and jams in a unique ecology of oneiric physics. Never overtly showy or overblown, there’s nevertheless a staggering level of ingenuity and synaesthetic effect to its detailed construction and gaseous fractals resembling the LSD or DMT experience. The label themselves compare its nuance to “the flicker of a candle over a desk of drum machines in a Midwestern basement, or the “first blush of sunlight over a tiny campground as subwoofers creak in the distance”, which proves a perfectly poetic analog to its digitally-smudged refractions and tongue-tip spectral tumescence. 

Ultimately, it’s a singular pleasure to immerse the senses in Topdown Dialectic’s self-contained soundsphere, and never more substantially so than on ‘False LP A’. Longtime enthusiasts will surely recognise his skill in parsing salient aspects of Basic Channel x Rhythm & Sound, and their descendants in Vladislav Delay or Pole, reframing those templates in far more uncertain space with a real animist magick. Each work feels tangibly, ambiguously alive, breathing with dynamics and more voluminous, macro scales, and iridescent with voices and details that commands attentive listeners who will have a field day zoning in/out to its illusive, holographic projections and syncopated chronics.
items._genre: dub techno / experimental electronic / ambient / IDM
items._cn_summary: Topdown Dialectic的首张全长专辑在False Aralia厂牌发行，收录了十六首各为五分钟的曲目，总长八十分钟。制作人Izaak Schlossmann以十余年的积累为基础，模糊了未发行素材与即兴片段之间的边界，营造出梦境般的物理感与有机生命感。评论指出其音乐继承自Basic Channel与Rhythm & Sound的dub techno谱系，同时以Vladislav Delay、Pole为参照，在更不确定的空间中重新框架化这些模板。每首作品在动态呼吸与宏观尺度中膨胀，细节与声音在全息般的投射中若隐若现。低频质感与气体般的分形纹理贯穿始终，被比作中西部地下室里鼓机之上的烛光闪烁，或远距离低音炮在露营地拂晓时的低鸣，形成一种催眠式的、解离的声学世界。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — One could say that everything was building up to the emergence of Starsailor, like the base of a massive pyramid tapering to a razor-sharp point, at once provocative and evocative, where Tim found the true meaning of his existence. Psychology speaks of the "primal scream" for good reason; sometimes, one must undergo a certain process, a cathartic one, perhaps, to reach one's destination. Tim Buckley's destiny lay in the stars, yet he had to get there by traveling a long road; folk and jazz guided him toward that atonal, distorted, avant-garde present where he built his sanctuary alongside his inseparable partner, Lee Underwood.In Come Here Woman, John Balkin played the bass furiously, while Lee Underwood experimented on guitar with dark, almost operatic flamenco-style melodies, and then Tim began to sing, as he never had before... and never would again. A singular shooting star that, if you didn't see or hear it... you missed it.Then the music kicks in, and you have to jump on board, it's rock 'n' roll, too; the percussion and guitar take on a jazzy, yet atonal, quality, as does the electric piano. It's all a storm that catches us by surprise, blink, and you'll miss it."I Woke Up," accompanied by the horns, feels like waves crashing against the beach sand and receding; the muted trumpet and double bass are the perfect companions. Tim's voice shifts, sometimes a tenor, other times higher-pitched, but it is always exactly right, creating a relaxed summer vibe even amidst this strange, dreamlike atmosphere. Throughout the album, we never quite know what time or place we inhabit, yet we know we are truly there."Monterey" is an acoustic rock track, with jazz undertones, where Tim's voice takes the place of the electric guitar and its solos. It features peaks and valleys, ranging from whispers to moments where his voice, striking a high note, sounds almost like a saxophone. He is like a Californian Peter Hammill; while Lee Underwood kept the guitar going with ceaseless repetition, it was Tim who handled the variations. Far from being chaotic improvisation, there was indeed chaos, yet it was a chaos driven by melody, moving perfectly toward its climax."Moulin Rouge" is a lovely interlude sung in French, showcasing the beautiful voice he was known for, accompanied by the trumpet. "Song to the Siren" and "Jungle Fire" represent two extremes of his vocal range, the former restrained yet outwardly expressive, the latter a long build-up culminating in an explosion alongside the band, where his voice truly functioned as just another instrument amidst wild, guttural, and primal improvisation. This trajectory leads to the title track, "Starsailor," which evokes a space-like atmosphere, one that feels as though it is tumbling into a black hole, featuring vocal stylings that range from Zappa-esque lows to Hammill-esque highs, yet serve a vastly different purpose; the mood steers the song toward a progressive sound, far removed from the jazz style found at the album's start.The Healing Festival revisits free jazz, pure double bass and saxophone, with Tim himself singing, stretching his voice and warping it like a rain-soaked blanket that changes shape once it's wet. "Down by the Borderline" ends with a flamenco flair, just as it began, but featuring the trumpet. Then the guitar kicks in with an unstoppable groove, joined by the drums and Tim, who is practically prancing with sheer delight just listening to them set the stage. He launches into the song with all his heart and lungs, following a syncopated rhythm; his vocal delivery is intentionally jagged, full of deliberate pauses and breaks, and in those gaps, a different path is paved: the path of Starsailor, his finest album, a record that could take him all the way up to the clouds, where it never rains.
items._genre: avant-garde folk / experimental jazz / progressive rock
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑将民谣、爵士、前卫摇滚与无调性实验融为一体，以粗粝吉他、钢琴、贝斯、管乐和自由变化的鼓点营造动荡而陌生的声场。蒂姆·巴克利从克制吟唱跨越到尖锐高音、嘶吼与近似萨克斯的滑音，令嗓音成为可即兴演奏的乐器。作品既有夏日般的松弛感，也不断坠入黑洞般的幽暗与混乱；旋律却始终牵引着结构，使失控感最终汇聚成高潮。其价值在于突破传统民谣与摇滚的边界，展示人声、乐队编制和空间氛围所能抵达的极端。

items._cn_summary: 法国具体音乐大师帕尔梅贾尼的12碟套装合集由INA GRM再版发行，收录其1964至2007年间绝大部分具体音乐创作。专辑跨越四十余年，从早期磁带实验到成熟期的电子声学作品，呈现其从皮埃尔·谢费尔门下起步、自成体系的创作脉络。具体音乐以日常声音素材为基础，通过剪辑、拼贴、变速、滤波等手段重塑声景，帕尔梅贾尼在此领域发展出独特的空间感与时间结构意识。合集中既有纯器质性声学作品，也包含与影像结合的多媒体创作。INAGRM作为法国国家音频研究机构的厂牌，以档案级品质重新整理并呈现这批作品，为具体音乐这一实验音乐传统提供了系统性的聆听入口。

items.body: The Polish band Jude was founded in 1993 and gradually earned recognition within the wider Experimental and Industrial music scene. “Zakaz” was originally released in 2024 by Kulturkampf, but two years later Zoharum is giving the album a welcome reissue aimed at collectors. Alongside the CD edition, it is now also available on vinyl. I missed the original release, but this reissue finally gave me the opportunity to discover “Zakaz”, and the least I can say is that it is a masterpiece of its genre. This is brutal, archaic Industrial music, with the guitar playing a central role alongside the relentless Industrial drums. The Polish vocals sound utterly possessed, perfectly matching the raw violence of the compositions. More than once, the album reminded me of the early work of Swans, yet Jude sounds even heavier, more intense, and even more merciless. The tracks surge forward without offering a moment of relief, at times drawing the listener into an almost trance-like state. Guitar and percussion merge into a powerful symbiosis that is impossible for devotees of the genre to resist. This is Industrial in its purest form-stripped of unnecessary embellishments and driven by raw, elemental power. (Rating:8½). Listen to “Beton Blok. Methodology”: Beton Blok. Methodology by Jude About Jude Jude is a Polish industrial and experimental act from Łódź, formed in 1993. The lineup has included Anna Krupska, Jacek Walczak, Konrad Grajner, Łukasz Franek and Wiktor Skok. The band’s discography includes “Combat Exhaustion” (2004), “Stat” (2015), “Ultimate Obedience” (2016, reissue and remaster) and “Pigment” (2017). “Zakaz” was first released on CD and digitally by Kulturkampf in 2024. Zoharum reissued the album in 2026 on CD and vinyl, with Kamil Łazikowski credited as recording engineer, mixer and producer on the original sessions.
items._cn_summary: 波兰乐队Jude的《Zakaz》原由Kulturkampf于2024年发行，2026年由Zoharum再版并首次推出黑胶。专辑以吉他与工业鼓机的核心编配构建压迫性声音空间，波兰语演唱呈现出近乎癫狂的原始张力。整体风格接近Swans早期作品，但更为沉重、密集且毫不妥协，层层推进的段落偶尔将听众引入近似恍惚的状态。吉他与打击乐的深度融合构成纯粹工业力量的表达，剥离一切多余修饰，仅保留元素性的暴力与重复律动。Zoharum作为东欧地下厂牌，为收藏者提供了这一重塑工业美学的珍贵载体。

items.album: The Remains: Short-Run Regional Releases from the Lao People's Democratic Republic
items.excerpt: Colour us enchanted with this otherworldly hour of airborne flute, Saw-U, vocal and drum spirits sourced from the night markets, museum shops and cafés of Laos, by Gary Sullivan ov Bodega Pop, who aptly compares them with Laurent Jeanneau’s forays in the same zone of interest for Akuphone & Sublime Frequencies. items.body:
Colour us enchanted with this otherworldly hour of airborne flute, Saw-U, vocal and drum spirits sourced from the night markets, museum shops and cafés of Laos, by Gary Sullivan ov Bodega Pop, who aptly compares them with Laurent Jeanneau’s forays in the same zone of interest for Akuphone & Sublime Frequencies. Check for the uncanny frissons of ‘Lam Cheung’ and its slew of piquant percussive works, all shimmering with the type of timeless lustre we’ve come to expect from Sullivan & DINTE’s magpie picks...

"In Lao PDR, music was seemingly everywhere. Walking through an open field outside Savannakhet to the sound of someone playing a khaen on a distant porch, the bracing rush of electronic molam from of one of Vientiane’s many aging malls, the awkward blending of the blind so u player’s voice with the bustling sounds of Luang Prabang’s night market.

It was in that UNESCO World Heritage Site that I found most of the CDs and CD-Rs from which I’ve ripped the tracks for this compilation. I’m almost certain I picked up a thumb drive at the night market that held many hours of additional music that could have been included, but if so, I’ve misplaced it, lost it for good, or simply misremember purchasing it in the first place. What I do remember is that these discs were literally the last copies in the cafe, museum, bookstore, and night market where I bought them, and not all of them played all the way through without sonic deterioration.

The sounds compiled here play in stark contrast to the more contemporary recordings I found in Laos, most of which featured some form of upbeat digital workstation molam or children’s songs. In addition to the ever-present khaen, this collection includes recordings of the sanai, a single-reed instrument fashioned from a water buffalo horn, the ceremonial khong nyai gong, the pi and similar free-reeds, and at least a dozen more traditional instruments played by Lao and ethnic minority artists. While some of these tracks were laid down in Vientiane or Luang Prabang, most were recorded near where the artists lived, from the legendary Vat Phou in the far south to the former Pathet Lao capital Xam Neua in the northeast.

Unlike Laurent Jeanneau’s more focused Lao collections for Akuphone and Sublime Frequencies, which remain among my favorite albums of all time, the present cassette-only selection is literally all over the PDR map. The sequencing is entirely in response to rhythm and texture and includes recordings from the 1970s, 80s, 90s, and early aughts. This may frustrate those with more of an ethnomusicology bent, but my hope is that the listener experiences something akin to wandering for the first time through this majestic country, encountering the last copies of forgotten recordings one after another, and hearing in these remains fragments of the past and a living musical landscape."

–Gary Sullivan (Bodega Pop)”
items._genre: world music / traditional Lao / ethnomusicology / field recording
items._cn_summary: 这是一张由Gary Sullivan（Bodega Pop）策划的老挝人民民主共和国地方唱片合集，素材来源于他在琅勃拉邦夜市、咖啡馆、博物馆商店寻得的稀见CD与CD-R光盘。合集以风笛（khaen）为核心，涵盖水牛角单簧管萨奈、仪式用孔尼鼓、pi等自由簧乐器，以及老挝本土与少数民族艺术家的演奏，横跨七十年代至千禧年初的录音年代。编曲逻辑完全以节奏与质感为出发点而非民族音乐学框架，呈现出散点式的听觉旅行感——从南部的瓦普寺到东北的前巴特寮首都桑怒。整体质感与Laurent Jeanneau为Akuphone和Sublime Frequencies制作的更聚焦的老挝系列形成对照，后者是Sullivan个人最爱的唱片之一。本作是磁带限量发行，强调田野录音般的真实与脆弱。

items.body:
The incomparable Winos dial-up a near-future fraught with glitching techno x surrealist folk artefacts supposed by mainman Morgan Buckley and his pal Ben Donohoe, a 12-track guess-again sprawl ranging from Arthur Russell-esque mood music to screwed Aphex jams.

Under the auspices of “Sworx”, an omniscient dialup modem, they parse coded waveforms in a discrete filing system, combing and recombining its data in a dozen buzzing post-techno chimeras and itchy electro jams. It’s instant classic Wah Wah Wino, freakishly playful and exerting odd sidespins on familiar styles and patterns with a ludic moxie that makes all their music so appealing.

The ‘Sworx’ system speaks its piece in a unique voice of detuned twangs and ululating electronic rhythms, shifting mercurial from what sounds like The Necks doing electro with a prepared piano on ‘OpportuniXt’, to a standout electro zinger with early AFXian vocaloids on ‘The System Works’, and Plone-esque key clatter on ‘dxmmy. pxtsy. rolodex’, thru a centrepiece calling to mind Oval’s most sublime on ‘breathwx (half_life)’. 

‘Western_intel [ frontier 2056 ]’ projects an unusually optimist vision of futurism, less techno dread, more cyber-pastoral, and the trip continues to wend from displaced, outernational folk in ‘Langley Prayer Room 9’, to a masterstroke of pitchbent club sauce in ‘sWORxism_noclocks_notimekept’ that tickles rarest pleasure centres with its piquant wrong-notes and gooey groove.

Collect them all!
items._genre: experimental electronic / glitch / post-techno / electro / avant-folk
items._cn_summary: 这是Winos厂牌旗下的一张实验电子专辑，由Morgan Buckley与Ben Donohoe合作完成。整张作品以虚构的调制解调器系统'"Sworx"'为概念框架，将编码波形视为可拆解重组的数据，在十二首曲目中构建出一系列嗡嗡作响的后科技舞曲混合体与不安分的电子碎拍。制作手法上大量使用失谐拨弦声、颤动的电子节奏，以及类似处理过的钢琴采样，呈现出从Arthur Russell式氛围音乐到扭曲Aphex Twin碎拍的超现实民谣质感。专辑中既有早期AFX式人声合成器的电光闪烁，也有Oval式的数字美感段落，并在'Western_intel [ frontier 2056 ]'中勾勒出一种罕见的乐观未来主义图景，融合了错位的跨国界民谣元素与弯曲音高的俱乐部律动，整体在熟悉的风格模式上施加奇异的侧旋，创造出独特的听觉体验。

items.body:
Munich’s modern art gallery Museum Brandhorst field wide ranging responses to an exhibit of works and concerts focussed on the works of John Cage, Merce Cunningham, Jasper Johns, Robert Rauschenberg and Cy Twombly, ranging from the sound poetry of Sofia Biazzi; to the sublime levitations of Maria Margolina; avant ambient pop of water lily; the pulsating technoid attack of focus baby; andCaroline Kretschmer’s subaquatic intrigue.

“Museum Brandhorst has invited Sound and Experiment to create a series of performances, audio works, and concerts in relation to the exhibition Fünf Freunde: John Cage, Merce Cunningham, Jasper Johns, Robert Rauschenberg, Cy Twombly. The event took place on June 27, 2025, as part of the Junge Nacht and the opening night of the annual Kunstareal Fest in Munich. The program featured newly produced pieces by Sound and Experiment participants Sofian Biazzi, Ilinca Fechete, focus baby, Daniel Gianfranceschi, Bruno Haas, Caroline Kretschmer, Bradley Leonard, Camilla Metelka, Maria Margolina, rosi and water lily. 

In a preparatory, biweekly seminar, discussions addressed conditions such as spectrotemporal displays, sharing time and frequency domains with different sound pieces simultaneously, and eventual performance constellations. An additional point of departure was a close reading of the indirect role of American artist David Tudor in some of the positions exhibited in Fünf Freunde, the function of the organization E.A.T. (Experiments in Art and Technology), and auditory scene analysis and synthesis in general.

The pieces featured on this CD are related to the presented performances, yet newly produced and with the audio CD format in mind.”
items._genre: experimental / sound art / avant-garde / contemporary composition
items._cn_summary: 慕尼黑现代艺术博物馆Brandhorst邀请Sound and Experiment系列，围绕John Cage、Merce Cunningham、Jasper Johns、Robert Rauschenberg与Cy Twombly的展览主题，委托多位艺术家创作全新音频作品与现场演出。艺术家们以Cage为代表的实验精神为起点，将声音诗、氛围流行、技术脉冲攻击、潜水式声景等截然不同的路径并置呈现。准备阶段的双周研讨会涉及频谱时域分析、美国艺术家David Tudor的间接角色、E.A.T.（艺术与技术实验）组织功能以及听觉场景分析等议题。专辑收录的作品虽与现场演出相关联，但专为CD音频格式重新制作。整体呈现是一次从视觉艺术展览延伸至声音实践的跨媒介探索，涵盖声音诗、氛围流行、Techno式冲击与水下式声响等多个维度。

items.body:
Anyone obsessed with those two incredible ‘Begena Songs…’ comps on Death Is Not The End will be properly enchanted by this more expansive - yet still intimate - suite of snapshots from Ethiopia, 1971, spanning the unique, twanging harp sound thru to Amharic poetry, chants, and spellbinding flute dances...

One that catches the breath with seldom felt sensations, ‘Ethiopian Musics 1971’ patently owes as much to the incredible performers as their faithful representation in Ragnar Johnson & Ralph Harrisson’s recordings. All secreted to tape on a Uher Report L stereo reel-to-reel recorder, they epitomise an era of ethnomusicological preservation, when the likes of labels such as Lyrichord and  Folkways were already decades deep “in the field”, documenting long-held traditions practically untouched by an encroaching, western modernity. And perhaps most crucially, the recordings beautifully render the acoustic settings and vivid vibes with an immersive quality in stark opposition to the era of dry, so-called audiophile studio recordings of ethnic musics to come - all the better for immersing in this wonderfully unfamiliar world.

The abundance of singular tones and strong, rare feels they produce is quite staggering to our northern english ears, and we reckon also for anyone else, for that matter. Opening to a joyful couplet of a bluesy ’Song about the beauty of women’, and the almost shanty-like swing and hard rhythm of ’Tej Beit Song’, the set reels to distinctive pieces of Ethiopian Christian song set to begena, or ‘Harp of David’, buzz, and a landscape-scale, 13 minute ‘Love Song (Mary Armede)’. A gripping ‘Drum Song (Jigsaw)’ will be mana to rhythm fiends, and a number of standout flute pieces reprise the frisson of our first encounter with this discipline on Sublime Freq’s ‘Staring into the Sun - Ethiopian Tribal Music’ set of 2012, most potently on the pluming twin pipes of the ‘Fila Flute Dance’ parts, whilst the pentatonic craar (6-stringed lyre) parts surely strike nerves for lovers of the rawest blues, and hail the liberated legacy of Mary Armede, a folk singer-fashion designer of Azmari heritage who surely warrants further investigation. 

No doubt this is one of the most striking archival discoveries of 2026, acutely advised to anyone enchanted with music from this corner of the world from Éthiopiques to begena harp, thru to Ragnar Johnson’s other arenas of research for Ideologic Organ in Yemen or Papua New Guinea. Dive in without delay.
items._genre: Ethiopian folk / field recording / ethnomusicology / harp music / flute
items._cn_summary: 这是一张1971年由Ragnar Johnson与Ralph Harrisson在埃塞俄比亚实地录制的民族音乐档案集，使用Uher Report L立体声开盘录音机完成捕捉。内容横跨贝吉纳竖琴拨弦、阿姆哈拉语诗歌吟唱、基督教宗教歌曲以至笛管舞曲等多种形式，涵盖13分钟的长篇情歌与节奏鲜明的鼓乐段落。录音保留了原始声学空间感与现场氛围，与后来干燥的演播室民族录音形成鲜明对比。专辑涉及begena竖琴、craar六弦里拉琴、双管笛等本土乐器，展现了阿兹玛里传统中歌手Mary Armede的音乐遗产。整体呈现1970年代民族音乐学田野录音的黄金质感，强调对未被现代性触及的音乐传统的忠实记录。

items.body:
Derek Bailey, Loren Connors and Bill Orcutt fiends will be in their element with Nathan Roche’s 2nd salvo of experimental twangers for a resurrected Celluloid; the legendary label with roots in post-punk & NYC mutations, who would also  issue ‘The Lambada’ - the biggest selling global single of ’89.

Hailing to France, via Townsville, North east Queensland, and Sydney, Australia, Nathan Roche has carved out an uncompromising catalogue of guitar abstractions since the ‘00s with myriad outfits, including turns on Siltbreeze, London’s World of Echo, and France’s excellently titled Gone With The Weed label.

After helping reboot the Celluloid label with his very psych-garage-rock LP ’35 Rue du Théâtre’ in 2025, the dozen succinct bits of ‘aa in reverse’ mark a sharp departure from the classic composure of his previous works, and into fractious deconstructions of blues guitar vernacular, very much in the vein of iconoclasts, Derek Bailey, Bill Orcutt, or Tetuzi Akiyama, but accented with his own twang.

In this abstract blues mode Nqthqn reserves the right to really jangle and pluck the listener’s nerves in tart, prickly expressions that favour microtonality and dissonance over more consonant, Western pleasures. The warp and weft of his material snags from the off with the distended notes of ‘astra’ thru the rudely detuned mix elegance and grunt in ‘aa’, pulling into Loren Connors-esue midnight melancholy on ‘aka’ and relatively stretching out into 3 mins of curdled to finely melodic chops on ‘adversary’.
items._genre: experimental guitar / free improvisation / avant-garde / blues deconstruction
items._cn_summary: 澳大利亚/法国吉他手 Nathan Roche 发布的第二张专辑是对布鲁斯吉他语汇的碎片化解构，十二段短小精悍的曲目以微分音与不协和音取代传统西方和声审美。从开篇延展的'astra'到粗粝失调的'aa'，再到带有 Loren Connors 式午夜忧郁的'aka'，以及相对伸展达三分钟呈现凝练旋律碎片的'adversary'，整张专辑在刺耳的拨弦与微音程张力中贯穿始终。作为曾于 Siltbreeze、World of Echo 等地下厂牌发表作品的资深实验吉他手，Roche 此番重启传奇后朋克与纽约变异音乐厂牌 Celluloid，延续了 Derek Bailey、Bill Orcutt、Tetuzi Akiyama 等前辈破坏传统的路线，同时融入个人的拨弦音色辨识度。专辑摒弃其前作经典构型，转向对布鲁斯传统的尖锐拆解。

items.body:
Late, great Finnish maverick Mika Vainio’s debut ’94 minimal techno masterpiece, originally conceived as Ø, is treated to a much needed reissue, newly expanded with all tracks from the CD on vinyl for the first time and including the absolute all-timer ‘Lasi’ - 100% unmissable if you know what’s good.

Back in circulation 20 years square since the 1st vinyl edition, and just over 30 years since the CD, ‘Metri’ serves a stone cold but heart-melting reminder of Mika’s way with puristic electronics. All 15 tracks from the CD are now cut to vinyl for a definitive edition of Mika’s exemplary solo statement, which would arrive the same year as his debut with Pan Sonic (the ‘Panasonic’ EP). It would dovetail with a time when the original Chicago, NYC and Detroit house and techno templates were being morphed in translation by new waves of artists such as Mika and his pal Ilpo Väisänen, or the likes of Richie Hawtin or Dan Bell, who all effectively streamlined the tekkerz of DJ Pierre, Blake Baxter and Rob Hood to even more stringent levels. 

What distinguishes Mika’s debut as Ø from all of the above is his feel for frosted tone and edge-of-distortion bite, rendered wth resounding plangency; all perhaps stereotypically reflective of his subarctic climes and expressing a sonic personality that would come to define certain strands of electronic music for decades to come, before his untimely passing in 2017, and ever since. We’ve lost count of the times the breathtaking motif of ‘Lasi’ has prompted us to a heads-down, air-punching jack, and reduced rooms at the afters to wide-eyed silent awe, until someone has to ask for an ID. 

Along with the likes of body-bouncing pulse and mind-bending acid tone to ‘Kuvio’ and ‘Twin Bleebs’, the uncanny amniotic ambience of ‘Radio’ and border-watch ambient tension of ‘Kenttä’, or the prototypes for his pure noise works in the ‘JL-CSG’, thru the sublime tension of ‘Dayak’, it’s every bit the ultra classique and we envy anyone coming across this album for the first time. Like many others, we will be taking the opportunity to replace well worn copies with a freshie to rinse and repeat for decades to come.

Seriously this one’s going to the grave with us.

items._cn_summary: 这张芬兰音乐人Mika Vainio以Ø名义发行的1994年首张专辑《Metri》迎来再版，首次将CD全部15首曲目完整压制为黑胶。乐评追溯了作品诞生的历史语境，将其置于芝加哥与底特律house、techno模板在欧洲被重新诠释的潮流之中，与Pan Sonic、Richie Hawtin等同时代艺术家的极简化路径相提并论。文章重点描述了作品的声响特征：边缘失真的咬合感、霜冻般的音色质感，以及源自亚北极气候的冷冽氛围。具体曲目方面，'Lasi'被描述为拥有让人俯首、拳头高举的强烈律动动机；'Kuvio'与'Twin Bleebs'展示了脉搏式低音与酸性音色的结合；'Radio'呈现羊水般的环境氛围；'Kenttä'带有边境监视式的紧张感；'JL-CSG'则预示了他后来的纯噪声探索方向。

items.body:
Barcelona-based Argentine sound artist Dima uses mythology to re-examine her personal world on 'Salva', dissolving instrumental phrases with confounding granular processes and allowing fragile trip-hop-inspired songs to emerge from the ambiance.

There's an unexpected balance on 'Salva'. At first, on the opener 'SOELAR' or its breathy follow-up 'APOGEO', you might think you have it figured out, its atmospheric blend of plasticky flutes and sci-fi pads. But as the latter track hits its third act, something unexpected appears - Dima's voice was already there, haunting the soundscape, but when a slowed-down beat joins it provides a real surprise. And 'Salva' keeps rocking from side to side, never settling into a reliable groove. On 'QUANTUM', Dima sings into an echoing void almost unaccompanied, but on 'FOLDING INWARD', she adds atmospheric synths and gong-y resonances to go in another direction, moving away from song structure towards grim abstraction. 

And after the one-two punch of the album's poppiest tracks, 'REACH' and 'IT HAD TO BURN', Dima concludes with 'Inked', a throbbing dark ambient nightmare that seems to dive deep beneath an alien ocean. Terrifying stuff.

items._cn_summary: 常驻巴塞罗那的阿根廷声音艺术家 Dima 以神话为棱镜，重新审视个人内心世界。她将乐器声部融入颗粒化处理过程，让脆弱的 trip-hop 风格人声从氛围纹理中浮现。专辑呈现出一种反复摇摆的不稳定结构：开场曲目以塑料质感的笛声与科幻合成器铺陈氛围，而当缓慢的节拍加入时，人声早已潜伏于音景之中；中段在不同曲风间反复跳跃，从近乎清唱的孤寂到充满黑暗抽象感的锣鸣共振；结尾则坠入深海的暗环境噩梦之中，以低频脉动收束全篇。整张专辑拒绝落入任何可预期的律动模式，在旋律与抽象、流行与实验之间持续游走，呈现出一个融合神话叙事与个人情感的独特声学空间。

items.body:
Steel-forged industrial brutalism from the Brum blast furnace of HALT, earning their Downwards stripes with a label debut that revels in dread tension and Midlands gloom somewhere between Scorn, Antonym, Karl O’Connor.

‘Slag Anthems’ cements Nathan Shwalbe & Craig Earp’s duo to the Downwards firm after Regis summoned them to the label’s 30th anniversary show at Birmingham’s Central, hosted amid familiar rogues; Surgeon, Russell Haswell, Mick Harris, Antonym and more. The specially packaged slab of heck builds on the solid foundations of 2020’s ‘Memory Fields’ LP for Erbium Records with a concentrated show of strength oozing from emulsified subs to plangent brutalist sound architecture, largely avoiding any regular drum patterns in favour of hulking offbeat structures and hallucinatory spectral silhouettes.

The duo’s native Brum is a presence and aesthetic muse throughout, prompting them to clash bin lids like duelling scimitars over pure bass effluence on ’Sassenach’, and lace their thrumming subs with a shiver of melodic glory on ‘Black Car’, or pull it all right down into Scorn-type mire on the recoiling drum play of ‘Rift Cantata’. A certain atmospheric levity to ‘Chernozem’ keeps it teetering just above an abyss they toe with macabre alacrity on ‘Pillars’, playing to a balance of black humour and uncompromising grit they tuck where the sun don’t shine on ‘I was just pleased to see you’.

Heavy.

items._cn_summary: 这是一张来自英国伯明翰的双人组合在传奇厂牌Downwards的首张专辑，以低频与工业质感为核心。二人刻意回避常规鼓点模式，转而采用笨重的离拍结构和带有幻觉感的声音轮廓，构筑出阴郁、压迫感极强的音景。伯明翰的工业城市气质贯穿始终：金属敲击声像兵器般碰撞，沉重低音中偶尔透出旋律性的闪光，鼓机节奏在泥泞沼泽般的质感中扭曲回缩。全作在黑色幽默与毫不妥协的粗粝之间寻找平衡，多首作品呈现出逼近深渊的张力。低频处理乳化模糊，氛围层次幽暗深邃，是面向地下场景的重型工业电子作品。

items.body: Bassist Alexander Frangenheim and saxophonist Stefan Keune belong to the third generation of European Improvised Music (or fourth, depending on how you calculate). I came across Keune and his trio with bassist Hans Schneider and drummer Achim Krämer with No Comment (FMP 2009), Frangenheim was on my radar because he was a member of Cecil Taylor’s Workshop Band ( Legba Crossing , FMP 1988) and later on he released several very good recordings on the Creative Sources label. Their musical style - not atypical for European Improv in the 1990s and 2000s - was more abstract than the recordings of the godfathers of this music which - while experimental - were often very concrete. Whereas concrete improvisation works with direct, tangible materials, situations, or predetermined rules - be they small melodies, energetic structures, or even a pure desire for destruction (one need only think of Peter Kowald’s and Peter Brötzmann’s “Kaputtspiel” phase - even if the latter disliked the term), abstract improvisation detaches itself from external circumstances to express feelings or states of mind primarily through sound, structure, and form. Abstractions are evident in many ways on New Traces , Frangenheim’s and Keune’s debut collaboration as a duo: first, in the pauses - moments of silence that are repeatedly interspersed among the music’s hectic passages, as in “New Traces 1” or “New Traces 7” - and second, in the music’s extreme density and concentration. Both musicians employ extended playing techniques such as harmonics, overtones, and percussive strokes. It’s not about melodies, but about exploring timbres, textures, and dynamic extremes. Ultimately, however, the abstract moments are most evident in the frenzied runs and competing trills, the contrasts in register (especially in “New Traces 4“, where they really reach the limit of what listeners can bear to hear), the impetuous stylistic drive, and the simultaneous clarity of the sound. True, Keune still hisses, coos, hums, and gurgles for all he’s worth, and Frangenheim scrubs away, making his bass weep and crash - yet it’s as if one had stripped Barry Guy & Mats Gustafsson’s Sinners, Rather Than Saints (No Business, 2009) of all its embellishments, oriental flourishes, vibratos, frills and obvious crescendos (don’t get me wrong, I love this album) - to draw a concrete example for comparison. Just listen to “New Traces 8“. Here, the improvisation takes unpredictable turns and surprising sounds are created, yet the structure of the piece remains crystal clear. A prerequisite for this is that both musicians have such an excellent technique that during the more frenzied moments, instrumental timbres coalesce without getting in one’s way. The album is a treat for fans of abstract music and sonic exploration. Very recommended. New Traces is available as a download. new traces by Frangenheim / Keune Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由低音提琴演奏者 Alexander Frangenheim 与萨克斯演奏者 Stefan Keune 合作，是两人首次以二重奏形式录制的作品。评论将两位音乐人定位为欧洲即兴音乐第三或第四代传人，并将其风格归入九十年代至两千年代欧洲即兴中较为抽象的一脉——与前辈具体即兴直接处理旋律、能量结构或破坏性冲力不同，这张专辑更多从音色、质感与动态极限出发，通过静默间隙、极端密度、高把位对比以及疯狂的连音竞奏来构筑抽象的声响世界。两人均大量运用泛音、泛列与打击性技法，萨克斯发出嘶嘶、咕噜、嗡鸣等非常规声响，低音提琴则被刮擦出哭泣与撞击的质感。评论特别指出，他们在激烈的段落中依然保持着结构的晶体般清晰，这要求双方拥有出色的技术控制力，使乐器音色在融合中互不干扰。

items.body: Review by alainPP — Aether, created in 2021 by four friends, initially began as a project for bassist Andrea's final thesis, with the aim of moving away from conventional jazzy sounds. Their sound blends post-rock, contemporary classical rock, and multi-layered jazzy prog."Oort Cloud" is a prime example, fusing ambient, jazzy tones, and dino-tinged progressive rock reminiscent of King Crimson, with a flute buzzing here and there. A long, contemplative suite encourages a dreamlike journey, with a primal Fender Rhodes piano accompanying the oppressive psychedelic guitar riff. "Vogon" opens with Collins' electronic drums, then shifts to a jazzier feel with Claudio Milano's frenetic narration. The air soars on Zappa-esque jazz-rock guitar in the purest tradition, flirting with the great Return To Forever on the distinctive piano; a frenetic finale with infectious energy. "Five Shades, Four Frames" opens with a spacey sound, a prominent rhythmic bassline. A drift into hyperspace follows this encroaching Crimson-esque crescendo; improvisation steers clear of interstellar notes. Midway through, the sound takes on an Arabic quality, reminiscent of a Star Wars desert, over a psychedelic Tangerine Dream melody. The obvious jazzy Rhodes turn on a drumbeat with a hint of Steven Wilson is surprising."The Melancholy of the Little Prince" features a melancholic piano drifting over percussion and electronic notes, giving free rein to the fretless bass. Musical scales, a crackling, distorted sound as if from a parallel universe. "Panta Rei" sees the flute searching for its footing, wandering notes for a learned musical digression; jazz, unmistakably King Crimson, Andrea's guitar surfing avant-garde territory for a controlled jumble. Dynamic and apocalyptic with its explosive contemporary finale, "Swerve" opens with a snowy, religious, ethereal feel. The captivating keyboards lead into post-rock territory illuminated by scores reminiscent of Porcupine Tree. The track then veers into jazzy soft rock territory with a distinctive piano demon unleashing a fury, recounting the new Italian sound.Aether brilliantly dares to create a jazzy post-rock fusion, injecting a dose of ambient and modern prog, opening this movement to the contemporary world.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由四位意大利乐手创作，最初源于贝斯手Andrea的毕业项目，旨在突破传统爵士乐的框架。作品将后摇滚、当代古典摇滚与多层次的爵士前卫融为一体，每首曲目都呈现不同的色彩与情绪。《Oort Cloud》以环境音与爵士律动为底色，King Crimson式的迷幻吉他riff与Rhodes电钢琴交织，营造出绵长的梦境感。《Vogon》在电子鼓点与爵士律动间切换，融合Zappa式爵士摇滚吉他与Return to Forever的钢琴传统。《Five Shades, Four Frames》从太空音效出发，经过King Crimson式渐强进入超空间，中段融入阿拉伯音阶与Tangerine Dream式的迷幻旋律。《The Melancholy of the Little Prince》以忧郁钢琴和无品贝斯展开异次元裂隙。《Panta Rei》让长笛自由游走于爵士与前卫摇滚之间。《Swerve》以宗教氛围的键盘开场，滑入Porcupine Tree式的后摇滚领地，最终以爆炸性的当代收尾。整张专辑在爵士后摇滚融合上大胆创新，注入了环境音与现代前卫元素，展现了意大利新生代乐手对这一音乐流派的当代诠释。

items.album: Amorphous interview: ‘Mono Substance’ and the body as reality check
items.excerpt: Brazilian-born, Brighton-based producer Gil OS released “Mono Substance” as Amorphous on 7 August 2026 through Semantics Productions. In this Amorphous interview for Side-Line Magazine, Gil OS speaks with Karo Kratochwil about the album’s core question, where the individual ends and the system begins, the role of Nora Avant’s voice across four tracks, bringing berimbau and alfaia into “Maracatu”, and testing an idea against the body before trusting it on recor
items.body: Brazilian-born, Brighton-based producer Gil OS released “Mono Substance” as Amorphous on 7 August 2026 through Semantics Productions. In this Amorphous interview for Side-Line Magazine, Gil OS speaks with Karo Kratochwil about the album’s core question, where the individual ends and the system begins, the role of Nora Avant’s voice across four tracks, bringing berimbau and alfaia into “Maracatu”, and testing an idea against the body before trusting it on record. Mono Substance begins with a philosophical problem, but Gil OS does not treat philosophy as something to paste over electronic music after the machinery has already been assembled. The interesting part is what happens when an abstract question, where the individual ends, whether separation is ever complete, how systems become internalised, has to survive bass pressure, repetition and a moving body. That line has been developing through Amorphous for some time. “Skepticism” looked outward at technology and the structures shaping human behaviour; “Devour” moved closer to consumption, obedience and the erosion of individual autonomy. On “Mono Substance”, Gil pushes underneath both questions and starts interfering with the boundary itself. If the individual and the system continuously shape one another, how useful is the distinction between them in the first place? Musically, however, “Mono Substance” is anything but an exercise in abstraction. Gil’s earlier history in chill out, freestyle electronics and psytrance remains somewhere inside his understanding of repetition and momentum, while Amorphous has developed a harder electro/EBM language of its own. Nora Avant’s voice enters the machinery on four tracks, while “Ancestors” and particularly “Maracatu” open the rhythmic vocabulary toward ancestry, ritual and collective physical experience. On the latter, Gil brings his Brazilian roots directly into the album through berimbau and alfaia, setting hand-played percussion against programmed electronics. Kratochwil had already seen how physical this music becomes when Gil performs it at Fourscher Festival. That experience became one of the starting points for the conversation that follows: control and surrender, melody as seduction, rhythm as communication, Nora Avant as another consciousness within the record, and why an idea that works perfectly in theory may still fail the moment the body refuses to believe it. Mono Substance by Amorphous Amorphous interview Karo: When I reviewed “Skepticism”, I was interested in the way you examined systems, technology and the structures that begin shaping the people who created them. “Devour” moved further into consumption, obedience and the erosion of self. On “Mono Substance”, the question seems to move underneath both of those subjects: where does the individual actually end and the system begin? Was that conceptual shift deliberate? Gil: Yes, I think that shift was deliberate, although it happened quite naturally through the work. With Skepticism, I looked outward at systems and technology, and with Devour, I became more interested in what those systems do to us through consumption and obedience. Mono Substance felt like the next step: turning the question inward and asking how much of what we think of as the self is actually our own. The line between the individual and the system becomes increasingly difficult to locate. At a certain point, the system isn’t just something outside us that we participate in, it becomes part of how we think, behave and understand ourselves. That tension is really at the centre of the record. Karo: The title “Mono Substance” immediately invokes the philosophical problem of whether apparently separate things are ultimately expressions of one underlying reality. What interested you in that idea musically? Gil: Musically, I was interested in the idea that very different things can emerge from the same underlying material. I wanted the record to explore that without trying to literally illustrate a philosophical idea. Rhythm, texture and sound became different ways of working with the same substance, repeating, mutating and breaking apart until something familiar starts to feel completely different. There’s also a tension in that: if everything comes from the same source, where does difference actually begin? Rather than adding a philosophical concept onto the music, I wanted the concept to exist within the way the sounds behave, develop and relate to each other. Karo: There is a fascinating contradiction between the album’s concept and its construction. Philosophically, the record questions separation, while musically your production is extremely precise, with sounds carefully differentiated and positioned. Did you ever think about the production itself as a way of exploring the difference between distinction and genuine separation? Gil: Yes, absolutely. Precision can create the impression that everything is clearly separated, but the more closely you listen, the more those boundaries start to blur. Sounds can occupy their own space while still being completely dependent on everything around them. Distinction doesn’t necessarily mean separation. You can isolate a sound, a rhythm or a texture, but it still exists within a larger system and is shaped by its relationship to everything else. In that sense, the precision of the production actually reinforces the central idea of the record rather than contradicting it. Karo: Before the current Amorphous sound, you had already travelled through very different electronic territories under Gil Mahadeva and Mukunga Umbura, including chill out, freestyle electronics and psytrance. How much of “Mono Substance” comes from allowing those older parts of your musical identity back into Amorphous rather than trying to maintain a strict electro or EBM vocabulary? Gil: I think those earlier projects are still present in the music, even if they’re not always obvious on the surface. I’ve always been interested in repetition, trance and the physical effect of rhythm, so those elements naturally found their way into Mono Substance. I wasn’t trying to return to those styles specifically, but I also didn’t want to exclude parts of my musical history just to maintain a strict Amorphous vocabulary. The older electronic work gave me a different understanding of movement and repetition. It’s less about genre and more about what certain sounds and rhythms can do to the body and the mind. Karo: One thing I have consistently liked about your work is that the intellectual element never becomes an excuse for the music to stop being physical. Do you consciously test an idea against the body, almost asking whether a concept still works once it has to survive a dance floor, bass pressure and repetition? Gil: Yes, definitely. For me, an idea ultimately has to work physically as well as intellectually. I can be interested in a concept, but if it doesn’t translate into rhythm, tension, movement or some kind of bodily response, then it probably doesn’t belong in the music. The dance floor is a useful test because repetition strips away a lot of the intellectual framing. You experience the sound first, and only later might you think about what it means. The body is almost the final reality check for the idea. Karo: Across the album, questions of control appear in several forms: political power, technological systems, consumption, conditioning and even control over one’s own perception. Yet musically there is also a strong tension between very disciplined programming and moments that feel more fluid, hypnotic or ritualistic. How much of that tension between control and surrender is built deliberately into the sound? Gil: Very deliberately. Control and surrender are two sides of the same process, especially in electronic music. Programming gives you an incredible level of control over rhythm, repetition and detail, but once those elements are repeated and layered, they can start to produce something that feels almost autonomous. There are moments where everything is tightly controlled and mechanical, and others where the repetition becomes hypnotic and you almost stop listening analytically and simply follow it. Surrender isn’t necessarily the opposite of control, sometimes it is what control eventually produces. Karo: Your music has become darker and more confrontational over time, but melody has never disappeared. Is melody important to you as a counterweight to aggression, or perhaps as something more dangerous, a seductive surface through which uncomfortable ideas can enter more easily? Gil: I think melody can do both. It can be a counterweight to aggression, but it can also make something much more unsettling because it gives the listener a way in. A melodic element can feel familiar or even beautiful while the material around it is much darker, and that contrast can make the underlying idea hit harder. If a difficult or uncomfortable idea arrives through something seductive, you may engage with it before you’ve had the chance to put up a defence. Karo: There is the hard electro and EBM impact I already associate with Amorphous, but also trance logic, more organic movement and, in places such as “Ancestors” and “Maracatu,” something communal or ritualistic. Is rhythm becoming a larger conceptual language for you, rather than simply the engine underneath the songs? Gil: Yes, I think so. Rhythm has always been central to the music, but on Mono Substance I became more interested in rhythm as a way of communicating rather than simply driving the track. With tracks like “Ancestors” and especially “Maracatu,” I was interested in that more collective aspect of rhythm: the idea that rhythm can connect people physically and almost temporarily dissolve the sense of the individual. Maracatu comes from the northeast of Brazil, particularly Pernambuco, and carries a strong Afro-Brazilian cultural identity, combining percussion, dance, ritual and community. I played the berimbau and the alfaia, the large bass drum that gives Maracatu much of its deep, powerful pulse, and then had to find a way of mixing and producing those organic instruments alongside the electronic elements. I wasn’t trying to reproduce Maracatu traditionally, but to let something from my own cultural background enter the language of Amorphous. Karo: Nora Avant appears on four tracks. On an album concerned with unstable boundaries and the idea that apparently separate voices may belong to the same underlying continuum, how did you think about bringing another voice into the record? Gil: Nora’s presence felt like much more than simply adding another voice. I think she became another consciousness within the record. Her voice has a very particular emotional and psychological quality, and that allowed the music to move into spaces I couldn’t reach through the production alone. At times she feels like a contrast to the machinery and repetition, and at other times she feels completely absorbed into it. I wanted her voice to become part of the same structure and, in a way, blur the boundary between the human and the system. Karo: I saw you live at Fourscher Festival, and what stayed with me was how little distance there was between the electronic construction and your physical performance. While making “Mono Substance”, were you already thinking about what these tracks would require from you physically when performed live? Gil: Yes, definitely. I don’t want the live show to feel like a reproduction of the record; it needs to have its own physical energy and sense of movement. The electronic elements can be very precise, but the performance introduces something human and unpredictable into that structure. For me, the ideal is that you don’t really perceive a separation between the electronic construction and the person performing it. Karo: Amorphous itself is a name that implies unstable form. Do you recognise one continuous line running through “Skepticism”, “Devour” and “Mono Substance”, even if you did not necessarily plan it from the beginning? Gil: Yes, I can see a continuous line running through it, even though I definitely didn’t plan the whole journey from the beginning. With Skepticism, I was looking at systems and the way they shape us. Devour moved closer to the individual and the way those systems can become internalised through consumption and conditioning. With Mono Substance, the question has become more fundamental: if everything is interconnected, can we really talk about the individual as something completely separate? The name Amorphous fits that process quite well, not because the music has no form, but because the form is always capable of changing. Karo: If boundaries disappear, connection becomes possible, but so do loss of autonomy, contamination and absorption into larger systems. Do you personally experience the idea of “one substance” as liberating, disturbing, or as a contradiction you deliberately wanted to leave unresolved? Gil: I think it’s both liberating and disturbing, and that contradiction is exactly what interested me. The idea that everything is connected can be comforting because it suggests that nothing exists completely alone. But if there is no real separation, then individuality and autonomy become much more complicated. I didn’t want to resolve that tension on the album. Mono Substance isn’t really arguing that unity is good or bad; it’s asking what happens to the idea of the self if we take that unity seriously. Karo: What happens now that “Mono Substance” is out? Are you planning live dates or a broader run of shows around the album? Gil: The first two shows were actually in Brazil, in São Paulo, which was very special to me. The CD was also sold there before it was available elsewhere and before the official release, so being able to present the album first in my own country felt like a huge bonus. I definitely want to continue bringing the album into a live setting. The challenge at the moment is finding organizers in Europe who are interested in having Amorphous perform live. I’ve approached a few people, but some haven’t responded, so I’m still trying to figure out how to make the live side more consistent and sustainable. The live version is also an opportunity to develop the more hypnotic and ritualistic side of the album. I want the set to feel physical, immersive and capable of changing in the moment. About Amorphous Amorphous is the solo project of Gil OS, a Brazilian-born electronic producer active since the early 1990s. Gil OS first made his name as the mastermind of Morgue Mechanism, one of the pioneering industrial and EBM acts in South America, released through the German label Off Beat. He later relocated to the United Kingdom, settling in Brighton, and worked under further monikers including Gil Mahadeva and Mukunga Umbura across chill out, freestyle electronics and psytrance before consolidating his electro-industrial work under the Amorphous name. Amorphous released the album “Shapeshifting” in 2016, followed by the “Behaviourism” EP, “Moth Metaphor” (2020) and “Stigmergy”. Side-Line has covered the project twice before through Karolina Kratochwil’s ‘Click Interview’ series, first in 2017 and again in 2020. The album “Skepticism” followed on Semantics Productions in 2024, previewed through the single “Algorithm“. On 19 June 2026, Amorphous released the single “Devour” featuring Nora Avant on main and backing vocals, written, produced, mixed and mastered by Gil OS. The track introduced the concerns of the forthcoming album in a club-oriented format. “Mono Substance” followed on 7 August 2026 through Semantics Productions, a ten-track album, Axiom, Devour, Masquerade, Blinding Gold, Domino Effect, Kingdom Fall, Ancestors, Unconditioned, Through The Noise and Maracatu, with Nora Avant providing backing vocals on “Devour”, “Blinding Gold”, “Kingdom Fall” and “Ancestors”, and artwork by Anastase Kyriakos. This interview follows Gil OS’ live performance at Fourscher Festival and marks Amorphous’ first Side-Line feature since the “Skepticism” campaign.
