items.body: Thirty years is more than enough time for an archive to become a mausoleum. This Morn’ Omina have little interest in building one. Vestiges – 30 Years of Ritual Sound (1996-2026) looks backward, certainly, but it does so according to the same logic that has always driven the project: material remains alive only as long as it can still move, change shape, enter a live set differently or find itself placed beside another piece from a completely different moment in the band’s history. That is why Vestiges does not behave like a conventional retrospective. Its selection moves through the Hegira and Nyan periods, older EP and vinyl material, pieces that have survived through changing live incarnations, and two previously unreleased versions that longtime concertgoers may already recognize. Mika describes it very precisely during our conversation: Vestiges is not a “best-of,” but a “part-of.” The distinction matters. This is less an attempt to establish an official history of This Morn’ Omina than to show which fragments of that history still carry current through the body of the project. And the timing makes that retrospective gaze particularly interesting. This Morn’ Omina are hardly standing still to admire their own past: Insha has opened another phase, Triptych and Rivers Of The Sea remain ahead, and the latter is intended to complete the Kundalini trilogy. After seeing the band at Castle Party this summer, where rhythm, bodies, light and concentrated physical energy seemed to occupy the same space, I wanted to talk to Mika about what thirty years actually look like from inside the project: memory, ritual, changing technology, old compositions that refuse to become fixed objects, and why the future still matters more than commemoration. This Morn’ Omina interview Karo: “Vestiges” is an interesting word for an anniversary release because a vestige is neither the past itself nor a complete record of it; it is what remains after time, change and disappearance have done their work. When you looked back over thirty years of This Morn’ Omina, what made something feel like a genuine vestige of the project rather than simply an important or successful track? Were you selecting music according to historical significance, personal memory, or according to what still feels alive to you now? Mika: Selecting these “traces” was based on the importance they have in the context of the past releases. Pierre St. Pierre was instrumental in the first draft of the list, as he listened for which ones might still prick up ears, and then the final list was created from a conceptual point of view so it would make sense on multiple levels. Karo: The selection does not behave like a conventional career retrospective. It refuses chronology and moves freely between different periods, while a substantial part of the core program comes from the Hegira and Nyan-era material rather than attempting to represent every phase equally. Was the intention therefore less to document what happened over thirty years than to identify certain ideas, rhythms and states of consciousness that have persisted underneath everything else? Mika: There is also a moral, ethical part at play. The Kundalini trilogy is still available as a physical medium and has not been finished yet. It would be dishonest toward the listener or buyer to try and sell the same tracks twice. So the focus went toward Hegira/Nyan, but also toward tracks from vinyls or EPs that are no longer available, while plenty of them are still, in rotating ways, part of the live sets. Karo: This Morn’ Omina has often organized music through cycles and larger conceptual structures, including the Hegira, Nyan and Kundalini sequences. A compilation necessarily removes individual compositions from those original systems and places them beside music that once belonged to another context. What happens to a ritual object when it is removed from the ritual for which it was created? Do these tracks retain their original meaning for you, or does Vestiges inevitably create a new mythology from fragments of the older ones? Mika: They retain their original meaning, although it could be argued that their closer links to the surrounding tracks on the original releases are missing. But now they are part of Vestiges, which is not a new mythology, just a compendium of different stories. Karo: There is an unusual tension between preservation and transformation here. Vestiges ostensibly looks backward, yet it opens with a previously unreleased version of “The Nameless Grey” and closes its 12-track core with the previously unreleased “One Eyed-Man (liber III).” Why frame an archive with versions the audience did not know from that history? Is there something important to you in refusing the idea that the past can ever be retrieved in one definitive form? Mika: These versions were always part of our live sets. We made them available for those people who have not been able to see TMO live yet, and for those who have and were asking where they could find these versions. Karo: That becomes particularly interesting with “One Eyed-Man,” because it is one of those compositions that acquired a life far beyond the circumstances of its creation and became an important point of recognition for This Morn’ Omina. The new “liber III” version means that thirty years are not concluded by preserving the familiar object in glass, but by opening it again. What can you hear in a composition after living with it for decades that its original author could not possibly have heard when writing it? Mika: “One Eyed-Man,” and other tracks as well, had many iterations because we like to keep the live situation interesting for us and for the returning live audience. They live a sonic life of their own and evolve according to our taste. Karo: The track titles themselves carry markings such as [ccf], [lcf], “liber II,” “liber III” and “FL.” On Vestiges, those designations become especially conspicuous because different systems and periods suddenly coexist on one tracklist. Rather than asking simply what the abbreviations stand for, I am interested in why classification has remained part of the language of This Morn’ Omina. Are these codes practical version markers, or do they also express the idea that a composition can exist in several states without one becoming the final, authoritative version? Mika: [CCF] is a term coined by a friend of mine, Paul Willeme, in 2000, when he noticed that the versions played live were shorter than those on the physical releases. He dubbed them “compressed commercial format,” and [LCF] “live commercial format.” These tags stuck throughout TMO history, as they clearly denote what to expect from that musical embodiment of that particular concept when released. “Liber…” can be seen as different “books,” self-sustaining entities. Karo: Rhythm presents another fascinating problem when looking back over thirty years. Electronic production technology has changed enormously since the earliest material, but the human body has not changed at anything like the same speed. This Morn’ Omina has always used repetition, percussion and pulse to produce states that are bodily before they become intellectual. When you revisit older pieces now, do you hear production methods that belong unmistakably to their time, or are you more struck by how little the fundamental mechanics of trance actually need technological progress? Mika: The writing process evolved over the decades, of course. But at its basis always lies the goal of inducing saccadic movement and attaining spiritual transcendence. Access to knowledge of new methods, or simply experimenting with different instruments or gear, old and new, makes rooting new concepts a pleasurable process as well. Karo: Your work has repeatedly brought archaic or pre-modern symbolic systems into contact with electronic machinery, from “Enuma Elish” and “The World Tree” to “Nuraghi,” while the music itself has moved through tribal percussion, industrial force, EBM and techno-derived repetition. After thirty years, do you still see an opposition between the archaic and the technological? Or has the project gradually demonstrated that both ritual and electronic sequencing rely on something very similar: repetition, pattern, anticipation and the transformation of consciousness through time? Mika: There has never been an opposition between archaic and technological in our worldview. All sounds work together to make the concept or the story of a piece intelligible and transmutable. Karo: There is a danger in the language surrounding “ritual industrial” that ritual becomes an aesthetic adjective: drums, symbols, incantatory voices, certain visual codes. This Morn’ Omina has always seemed much more concerned with what rhythm actually does. After three decades, what distinguishes ritual as a real compositional process from ritual as decoration? Is there a point at which repetition ceases to be a musical device and genuinely alters the listener’s state? Mika: A track is finished when everything has blended into one form that interconnects all elements, whether this is a voice, noise, hand drum or lower frequencies. The whole is ritual, not just one specific element. Karo: Vestiges also raises the question of memory in electronic music. A photograph or written document tells us something about a past event from a distance, whereas an old rhythm can make a body reproduce an action it performed twenty years earlier. When you hear these tracks together now, is your memory primarily intellectual, remembering studios, people and circumstances, or physical? Can the body remember a piece of music differently from the person who made it? Mika: I remember all of the circumstances in which these tracks were made. Most of them are good memories; some are tied to lesser ones because of, in most cases, failing gear or erratic musical experiments going off the rails. Listening to ritual music leaves an imprint on mind and body. That is a personal experience. The creator has no control over that. Karo: Earlier this year you described Insha as reflective rather than restrained, a necessary return to stability after a period in which This Morn’ Omina had effectively undergone a tabula rasa. That makes the timing of Vestiges particularly intriguing. Does an artist look at his archive differently after having seriously contemplated an ending? In other words, did almost losing the continuity of This Morn’ Omina change your understanding of which parts of those thirty years were actually essential? Mika: To an extent, yes, because of the necessary turmoil that is part of a tabula rasa. But Insha was not made on a deserted island. It was made on a peninsula, a place that, even though remote, is still firmly connected to the mainland. After Insha, it was with fondness that we looked back upon what had been made before. Karo: There is also a difficult curatorial question hidden inside every retrospective: exclusion. Eighteen pieces can represent thirty years only by leaving a vast amount outside the frame. Were the omissions harder than the selections? And did you ever reject a track precisely because it was too obvious, too successful or too strongly associated with one historical version of This Morn’ Omina to tell the story you wanted Vestiges to tell? Mika: Well, blame us for the omissions, hah! It was not hard at all to leave certain tracks out. Vestiges needed to make “sense” to listeners, new and old. Certain tracks did not make it, as otherwise it would have been too long to present in a meaningful way. So we apologize that “your favorite track” was not included. Karo: You have said recently that stories within This Morn’ Omina matter across past, present and future, and that many different sources can flow toward one larger universal arc. Listening to thirty years compressed into one collection creates an unusual opportunity to test that belief against the work itself. When you place a piece from 1998 beside material conceived many years later, do you discover continuity you consciously planned, or patterns that only became visible retrospectively? Can an artist discover meanings in his own catalogue that the younger version of himself never intended? Mika: There is continuity. But it is not rigidly planned. In the end, the person or people making it evolved over time, but it is still the same human being at the cradle. The production value definitely went up quite a few notches over time. Karo: There is a particularly beautiful paradox in releasing Vestiges during what is actually an extremely productive new period for This Morn’ Omina. Insha arrived this year, and you have already said that two further records are in development: Triptych and Rivers Of The Sea, with the latter intended to complete the Kundalini trilogy. Has the process of excavating these thirty years fed back into the music you are making now? I am curious whether an archive can work in both directions: preserving evidence of where you have been while quietly changing where you are able to go next. Mika: I do not see any paradox at all. Vestiges is a pebble along the same road where Triptych and Rivers Of The Sea will be. We could have waited another 10 years, but we decided not to. This Morn’ Omina has always had a prolific output because we feel that there are always new concepts that deserve the light of day, and maybe waiting another 10 years would have made a Vestiges project almost too big and therefore confusing. Vestiges is not a “best-of.” It is a “part-of.” Karo: I have to finish with the live side because I have just seen This Morn’ Omina at Castle Party, and it was an extraordinary visual and sonic experience. What struck me was how completely the music occupied the space: rhythm, bodies, light and the almost ceremonial concentration onstage seemed to become parts of the same thing. You still have several dates ahead, including the special 30th-anniversary performance at La Luna Obscura in Ostend, Fourscher Festival in Erfurt, and Schachtfrequenz in Zwickau in February 2027. Are further concerts being planned around the 30th anniversary and Vestiges, and is there anything particular you want these anniversary performances to say about where This Morn’ Omina is now, rather than simply celebrating where it has been? Mika: Thank you. We found it a resounding experience as well. A deep connection with the audience was formed through a TAZ. La Luna Obscura is the only real anniversary concert, with a one-off special setlist. The concerts that are lined up, and those not announced yet, will definitely reflect some parts of that, but our aim is the future, with new tracks and new stories to tell. About This Morn’ Omina This Morn’ Omina is a Belgian post-industrial and ritual trance project founded in 1996 in Roeselare by musician and producer Mika Goedrijk. Musically the project mixes ritual trance, tribal industrial, power noise and dark ambient, built around polyrhythmic percussion and layered atmospheres. In its early years, the project issued three self-released tapes on the Afterfurcht imprint: “The Future Has Taken Root In The Present” (1996), “Terra Tramuit et Quievit” (1997) and “Decline and Fall of Empires” (1997). These recordings led to the first full-length CD, “Nezeru Enti Sebauem Neterxertet,” on the Italian label Old Europa Cafe in 1997, followed by “Em Sauf Haa Heru” (1998) and “Taiu” (2000), completing the initial Hegira-related cycle. During the 2000s, This Morn’ Omina released a string of albums on labels including Ant-Zen and Spectre Records, among them “7 Years Of Famine,” “Le Serpent Blanc / Le Serpent Rouge,” “The Drake Equation” and “Les Passages Jumeaux.” The track “One-Eyed Man” became one of the project’s best-known compositions, giving This Morn’ Omina wider recognition beyond its ritual industrial base. In 2017, the project moved to the German label Dependent for the double CD “Kundalini Rising,” followed in 2021 by “The Roots Of Saraswati,” also on Dependent. In 2025, This Morn’ Omina released the four-track digital EP “Omm Of Life” through Zazen Sounds. Beyond This Morn’ Omina, Mika Goedrijk has been involved in several other projects, including Sygo Cries, Nebula-H, Pow[D]Er Pussy, Les Nuits Blanches, Project Arctic, Andraculoid and, more recently, Plan C. In January 2026, This Morn’ Omina announced “Insha,” released 23 February 2026 as a CD and digital co-release between Cyclic Law and Zazen Sounds, the project’s first new full-length album in five years and its twelfth studio album overall. In June 2026, This Morn’ Omina joined the Dark Dimensions Label Group and announced “Vestiges – 30 Years Of Ritual Sound (1996-2026),” a compilation of known, rare and previously unreleased tracks marking the project’s 30th anniversary, released as a limited edition digipak CD via ProNoize / Dark Dimensions on 26 June 2026. This Morn’ Omina played Castle Party in the summer of 2026 and has further dates ahead, including a 30th-anniversary performance at La Luna Obscura in Ostend, Fourscher Festival in Erfurt, and Schachtfrequenz in Zwickau in February 2027, with two further albums, “Triptych” and “Rivers Of The Sea,” in development, the latter intended to complete the Kundalini trilogy.

items.body: Although Robin Storey has been active with his Rapoon project for even longer, he will always be closely associated with Zoviet France. In 2001, the British artist released Cold War: Drm ‘N’ Bass, an album now celebrating its 25th anniversary with the addition of an exclusive third disc. The original double album was conceptual on several levels. Storey explored elements of D’n’B, fusing them with his distinctive musical universe, while also using the work as a personal reflection on the state of the world and contemporary geopolitics. That theme remains as relevant as ever and serves as the guiding principle of the new third disc, which draws its inspiration from today’s global conflicts. The world seems not to have changed for the better—if anything, it has become even more troubled—yet these developments continue to inspire artistic expression. The original album has lost none of its magic or power. It is Rapoon at its very best. Tribal influences emerge primarily through the rhythms, intertwined with the project’s familiar Eastern-inspired atmospheres. The music is dark, at times almost bleak, and enriched by the deep, low-end textures that characterize D’n’B. The new album features eleven tracks that echo the themes and ideas of the original compositions while leaning more toward Experimental music and Cinematic soundscapes. Atmosphere takes center stage, with the D’n’B elements receding into the background. Repetitive loops, Industrial textures, and wonderfully crackling samplings from radio transmissions are seamlessly woven together into an apocalyptic whole. I even detected a track with distinct Martial influences, which fits perfectly within the album’s overall concept. This is therefore far more than a straightforward reissue. It is a thoughtful reimagining of the original work, shaped by the turbulent events of recent years and given renewed relevance in today’s world. (Rating:8). Listen to “It’s Over Isn’t It?”: It’s Over Isn’t It? by Rapoon About Rapoon Rapoon is the solo project of English musician Robin Storey, based in Newcastle upon Tyne. Storey formed Rapoon in 1992 after the breakup of Zoviet France, the group he had been part of since 1980, using the new project to explore what he described as “ethnic musics” and techniques he felt he could not pursue with his former band. Most of Storey’s recordings in the 1990s appeared on Staalplaat and Soleilmoon, including “Raising Earthly Spirits” (1993) and “The Kirghiz Light” (1995). A 1996 US tour led to a connection with Matt Jacobson of Relapse Records, which released “The Fires of the Borderlands” in 1998. Rapoon’s “Cold War: Drum n Bass” first appeared as a double CD on Caciocavallo in 2001. Later releases include “Time Frost” (2007, Glacial Movements), “The Library of the Dead” (2008, Ewers Tonkunst), “Disappeared Redux” (2012, Zoharum) and “Cultural Forgeries” (2014, Alrealon Musique). In 2019, Storey discussed the project’s approach in a Click Interview with Rapoon on Side-Line. Zoharum, which had already released Rapoon’s “Disappeared Redux” in 2012, now reissues “Cold War: Drum n Bass” as a 3xCD edition, adding the new third disc reviewed here.

items.body: Statiqbloom Splintered Fingers self-released Fade Kainer’s Statiqbloom has two fairly distinct eras; the electro-industrial years spanning from the project’s foundation in 2014 to around 2020, and the more freeform era (the beginning of which coincided roughly with Kainer’s move to Berlin from Brooklyn) which explore industrialized techno, dark ambient, and rhythmic noise, amongst other sounds. New album Splintered Fingers situates itself between the latter styles handily, unifying them via Statiqbloom’s propensity for blackened textures and depressive ambience. Whether or not Kainer set out to split the difference on the album isn’t clear, but there are plenty of callbacks to his recent history, often reconstituted and recontextualized for effect. “Salt the Flower (stripped back version)” takes the noisy and clamorous cut from recent Hands Production release The Casket Nest and carves away the beats, leaving only reverbed drones, half-chanted vocals and ominous waves of feedback that threatens to drag the whole song under. It’s quite reminiscent of the work he was doing on Winter, although the extremity of its sound, shared by cuts like the brief “Threshold” and the thrumming “Sedated Presence” bring to mind his Kain LP for Sonic Groove. Still, Kainer is ever reluctant to sit still for any period of time, and there are hints of new directions sprinkled throughout the proceedings. Opener “Grave Procession” feels like a classic powernoise cut in its rhythm, but the thick layer of saturation that sits atop its relentless tempo has a sort of smothering tension to it, like the beats are slowly being churned into nothing as the song goes on. Alternately, on “Groundless” the slow tempo and funereal pads have the same sensibility as much of the witch house revival sound, albeit with a nod to the lo-fi sound of early black metal. While not new in terms of sonics, they’re certainly formations we haven’t heard Kainer try his hand at explicitly, and could easily prove to be fertile ground for the prolific artist. Like most of Statiqbloom’s 2020’s output, Splintered Fingers is about mood above all else; even on the record’s centerpiece track “H.O.M.K.V. (live)”, an eight minute excursion into some truly gnarly beats and shouted vocals, there’s a bleak strain of pained emotion that informs the proceedings. Regardless of whatever sounds Fade Kainer is trying his hand at, his particular brand of rage and woe will mark it as his own. items.album: Dead Voices on Air Finds Strange Forms Inside the Seams in New Album “Mothcomma”
items.excerpt: For nearly four decades, Dead Voices on Air has occupied a peculiar territory between industrial music, abstraction, improvisation, and the frayed edges of song. Mark Spybey has spent that time following ideas wherever they lead, accumulating a body of work connected less by fixed genre than by a willingness to pull recorded music apart and discover what might live inside its seams. His latest album, Mothcomma, continues that restless history. Released worldwide through Re:Mission Entertainment
items.body: For nearly four decades, Dead Voices on Air has occupied a peculiar territory between industrial music, abstraction, improvisation, and the frayed edges of song. Mark Spybey has spent that time following ideas wherever they lead, accumulating a body of work connected less by fixed genre than by a willingness to pull recorded music apart and discover what might live inside its seams. His latest album, Mothcomma, continues that restless history. Released worldwide through Re:Mission Entertainment on July 17th, Mothcomma began taking shape almost immediately after Dead Voices on Air returned from its 2025 US tour. Recording was divided between the Tees Valley in North East England and Lafayette, Colorado, with studio work and remote sessions allowing distance itself to become part of the process. Spybey was joined by Nathan Jamiel of Denver’s The Drood and DADU’s Stephen Weatherall, both of whom have become established members of the group after contributing extensively to the previous two albums and joining Spybey for concerts across the United States last autumn. Across Mothcomma, recognisable structures periodically surface before dissolving into stranger forms. Pas de Chasse moves with cinematic unease, while Eye Exhaust gathers layers into a dense, unsettled mass. For the Rush of Black Tar draws tension from repetition and texture, and the title track reaches toward something brighter and more expansive. Geography, memory and spontaneous decisions pass continually through the record, giving its disparate pieces an internal logic without sanding down their rougher edges. Spybey’s history offers plenty of precedent for such open-ended work. He began his career with Zoviet France in North East England during the late 1980s before relocating to Vancouver and founding Dead Voices on Air. He subsequently became an original member of Download alongside members of Skinny Puppy, providing the voice for 1996’s The Eyes of Stanley Pain. His collaborations have since included Graham Lewis of Wire, Faust, Michael Rother, Dieter Moebius, Jarboe, Lee Scratch Perry, James Plotkin, Robert Hampson, Jochen Arbeit, Martin Atkins and Genesis P-Orridge. Among the more remarkable chapters came through CAN guitarist Michael Karoli, who invited Spybey into Sofortkontakt! for CAN’s 30th anniversary concerts in 1999. A year earlier, Spybey had toured with Karoli as part of Damo Suzuki’s Network. His memoir, Explicit in Purpose, was published by Emergency Hearts in 2022, while recent years have also found him working with old friends in DADU. Alongside Mothcomma, the official Dead Voices on Air shop has now opened, bringing together releases and merchandise from Spybey’s extensive catalogue. The store includes CDs, vinyl, cassettes, autographed copies, out-of-print material, collaborations, side projects, new shirts and copies of Mothcomma. Some stock ships from the United States, while other items are dispatched directly by Spybey from the UK. The first 40 orders also receive a 3×3 Dead Voices On Air logo vinyl sticker. items._cn_summary: Dead Voices on Air 的新专辑《Mothcomma》延续了 Mark Spybey 近四十年来在工业、抽象与即兴边缘游走的创作脉络。录制跨越英国东北部 Tees Valley 与美国科罗拉多州 Lafayette 两地，远程协作与现场录音交替，使地理距离本身成为创作过程的一部分。专辑中可辨识的结构时常浮现又旋即消解于更陌生的形态——《Pas de Chasse》以电影式的不安感推进，《Eye Exhaust》将声音层次堆叠为致密而躁动的整体，《For the Rush of Black Tar》从重复与质感中抽取张力，标题曲则试图触及更明亮、更开阔的意境。地理、记忆与即兴决策贯穿整张唱片，使零散的段落获得内在逻辑而未被磨平棱角。Spybey 早年在 Zoviet France 起步，后参与 Download、Michael Karoli、Sofortkontakt! 等计划，合作名单涵盖 Faust、Michael Rother、Dieter Moebius、Jarboe、Lee Scratch Perry、Robert Hampson、Genesis P-Orridge 等。专辑由独立厂牌 Re:Mission Entertainment 于七月全球发行，同期开设官方商店整合其庞大目录。

items.body: Becoming a new person Leaving just a trace behind What Nationalists want to avoid That is what I do now Roman Wilhelm began making music in 1991 with the sort of recording setup that encourages either ingenuity or surrender: two ghetto blasters, a teenage bedroom, and no obvious reason to believe anyone beyond its walls would ever hear the results. Born in 1976 in a small West German town, Wilhelm had recorded his first song by the time he was fifteen. A demo tape eventually found its way to a local goth DJ, who invited him to perform at a small dark-music festival. There remained the practical matter of instrumentation. Wilhelm did not own a synthesizer, so he brought his Italian accordion. That solution says quite a bit about the sensibility behind roman946, Wilhelm’s long-running musical project, where the machinery of post-punk and electronic music has always been susceptible to interruption by something tactile, eccentric, or stubbornly homemade. The accordion was hardly an adolescent anomaly. During his years studying graphic design in Halle (Saale), Wilhelm began collaborating with aspiring filmmakers, composing music for images before gradually moving toward a broader conception of performance. After relocating to Berlin in 2005, he found himself drawn into the city’s art world, playing gallery openings and treating music, at times, as an exhibit with its own spatial and conceptual logic. His new album, Balta, gathers those seemingly separate histories into one body of work. Songwriting sits beside electronics; programmed structures are interrupted by acoustic instruments; post-punk economy brushes against folk music and experimental composition. Wilhelm cites Onuka, Laurie Anderson, Lou Reed, The Legendary Pink Dots, and And Also The Trees among his inspirations, a list broad enough to suggest that taxonomy has never been his preferred occupation. The album’s geography is equally expansive. Balta looks toward Germany and Eastern Europe at a moment when political anxiety has become increasingly difficult to leave outside the rehearsal room. Wilhelm addresses the rise of the political right in Germany, intolerance, artistic freedom, gender stereotypes, and the unease surrounding developments farther east, drawing much of the material from events he has witnessed and conversations with people whose lives intersect with these pressures. His working life gives those concerns an unusual proximity. Wilhelm divides his professional time between the German Institute of Economic Research and the Berlin University of the Arts, moving between debates over social policy and questions about artistic independence. Those worlds find their way into songs such as BBC and into the wonderfully peculiar phrase Lead me to Ambivalentopia, which may be as good a name as any for the continent Wilhelm is attempting to describe. Wilhelm speaks eloquently about his songs: The Beach (Daina #1) “The album begins with a Daina, a traditional Latvian genre of song and poetry consisting of four lines, often employing diminutives (Balta, balta debestiņa (little white sky), gaidu, gaidu vasariņu (waiting for the little summer), koki klusē vērojot (trees watching in silence), melnus kuģus jūriņā (black fleet in the little sea)). After the central motif, which uses cellos and guitars to evoke the motion of waves, addresses geopolitical uncertainties, the loud finale resolves the tension through absurd acts of defiance. The final line abruptly switches from English to French and Chinese.” The plodding beat and horns give this spoken word track a deep gravity, almost bordering on psychedelic. Aufbruch “A Jungle rhythm never fully unfolds in this song; repeatedly stutters to a halt, prompting uncoordinated flailing rather than dancing. The bass holds together elements that the piano, synths, and guitar seem unable to reconcile. Hovering over it all is the vocal, which also fails to strictly adhere to the beat. A German story of flight leads to the question of how the grandchild generation would treat refugees today; it identifies intolerant, right-wing behaviour as a negative dimension of flight. Both vocals and lyrics are indirectly influenced by Hildegard Knef and Nico Pfäffgen, particularly in the way they handle the interplay between banality and the dramatic. The song is based on an authentic poem about fleeing Silesia and the subsequent experience of social exclusion in the Federal Republic of Germany.” BBC “This simply structured post-punk theme, driven by a central guitar riff, centers on a person trapped in academic gender clichés.” Chimes and motorik beats bolster this track, which sounds like a lost Fad Gadget track. I Need Nida “A melancholic motif emerges, shaped by the imprecise playing of an analog synthesizer with faulty filters. We observe the protagonist, Katya, a dissident from Kaliningrad as she builds a new life as an artist in her adopted home of Armenia. The abrupt onset of the chorus underscores the fact that homesickness knows no borders. The song was inspired by a text message from the real-life Katya (I asked her where she was going, all she said is: I need Nida).” Ambivalentopia “Berlin-style electro-post-punk meets the stark juxtaposition of multilingual names for various border towns, some situated at the heart of current political events, others far detached from the global stage. The convergence of multiple languages seems to obscure the message, yet invites the listener to seek it out in the spaces in between: the dream of a world where one is no longer limited to simply choosing one out of several names.” This track has a heavily Kraftwerk-inspired chant and backbeat that will get stuck in your head. Exchange; KWC “Being an academic exchange coordinator for Berlin University of the Arts, I deal with the questions raised in “Exchange” on a daily basis: What is openness? How does tolerance emerge? Is time abroad mostly about partying? Where do you go? Is there an atmosphere of openness? Two verses present a caricatured juxtaposition of utopia and dystopia before the language abruptly switches to Chinese in the final chorus. With its hard, driving drum’n’bass sound, “KWC” contrasts sharply with the lyrics: a belated, self-reproachful letter to a deceased friend.” Hotel “An old clock sets the tempo for the album’s most oppressive track; an accordion and an electric piano seem to be chasing the seconds. It tells the true story of a hotelier in a small Saxon town who aggressively tries to justify to the narrator why he did not turn away a group of fascists arriving for a conference (After all, what was he supposed to do? Hardly anyone visited them anymore, and he was left alone with the fascists in the hotel). That clock is ticking very loudly right now, too, in the run-up to the elections in Saxony-Anhalt, where right-wing populist AfD is campaigning for an abolishment of compulsory education, and for the eviction of all foreigners, whoever they may be.” An Old Fort; Take This Town (Daina #2) “Listeners are taken on a spoken-word tour through the overgrown ruins of Kostrzyn (Küstrin). The concluding fragment, “Daina #2,” tells the story of a refugee from Ukraine currently in Latvia (We ordered drinks, I heard her say: “If I don’t drink, I can’t sleep”. Age seventeen). The musical concept, collapses in on itself at the end. Listen to Balta below and order the album here. items._cn_summary: 罗马946的新专辑《Balta》将后朋克、电子与手作器乐编织成一张横跨德国与东欧的音乐地图。Wilhelm早年用两台ghetto blaster和意大利手风琴起步的经历塑造了他独特的美学：后朋克的经济性不断被原声乐器和实验性作曲所打断。专辑以拉脱维亚传统歌谣形式Daina开篇，引入民间素材；BBC等曲目则融合了电子编程与社会议题。Wilhelm在经济研究所与艺术大学之间的双重职业背景为作品注入现实重量，涉及德国右翼抬头、性别刻板印象与艺术自由等议题。'Lead Me to Ambivalentopia'这一短语浓缩了整张专辑试图描绘的欧洲大陆的精神状态——一种在政治焦虑中无法定论的多义之地。制作上注重空间与概念逻辑，兼具画廊展演与专辑聆听的双重属性。

items._cn_summary: Nala Sinephro 这张专辑以一条贯穿全作的电子琶音为骨架，在十首曲目间构建出绵密而连续的宇宙感。作品延续并拓展了她首作中已显露的野心，将灵性爵士的冥想气质与氛围音乐的空间感融合为一。编曲上引用了 Alice Coltrane、Sun Ra、Jon Hassell 等前辈的精神遗产，但在节奏处理与和声延展上加入了更具当代性的电子思维，使音乐既有即兴的张力也有环境音乐的沉浸质地。专辑将灵性爵士的庄严感与氛围音乐的绵延感并置，人声与器乐在层次中交错推进，营造出沉思而开阔的听觉空间。

items._cn_summary: 这张由法国国家音响研究小组（GRM）发行的合辑收录了卢克·费拉里跨越六十年创作生涯的作品，时间跨度从1958年担任GRM创始主任开始。合辑以十张CD、近十一小时的容量系统梳理了具体音乐与电子音乐的演变轨迹，涵盖了他在不同阶段的声响探索与作曲实践。作为与皮埃尔·舍费尔、皮埃尔·亨利等具体音乐先驱同系列的重要文献，费拉里的作品聚焦日常声音的采集与重组，将环境音、录音素材与电子处理技术相结合，发展出介于音乐、声音艺术与田野录音之间的独特美学。整体呈现了一位二战后欧洲实验音乐代表人物的完整创作脉络，为研究二十世纪声响艺术的历史脉络与创作方法提供了不可多得的档案式聆听入口。

items.body: Label: Blue Note Records, 2026 Personnel - Charles Lloyd: tenor saxophone, flute; Zakir Hussain: tabla, percussion; Eric Harland: drums; Vijay Prakash: vocals; Rakesh Chaurasia: bansuri; Sabir Khan: sarangi; Niladri Kumar: electric sitar; Ranjit Barot: keyboards. Everyone knows that Charles Lloyd’s music is a sea of authenticity that lifts the spirit and awakens the senses. Most of the tracks on Sangam and Friends , his new album serving as a homage to the late tabla player Zakir Hussain, were recorded live in Mumbai in 2009 for an album that was never released. Drummer Eric Harland is the third side of the triangle that composes Sangam, yet this date is enriched by a rotating lineup of standout Indian collaborators that includes vocalist Vijay Prakash, bansuri player Rakesh Chaurasia, sarangi player Sabir Khan, sitar player Niladri Kumar, and keyboardist Ranjit Barot. As expected, the new album traffics in an outgoing blend of world fusion, avant-jazz, and post-bop that attains emotional peaks on “ Bharati’s Dance, Tempo Divine ” and “ Sam on the Ganges ”, a sprightly reimagining of Lloyd’s memorable tune “ Sombrero Sam ”. The former piece showcases Lloyd in top form, blowing impulsively and fabulously over Hussain’s entrancing tabla patterns and Harland’s smart drumming. This Indo-jazz breeze is also felt on the latter piece, where Barot’s keyboards reinforce the texture, paving the way efficiently for bansuri and tenor discourses. Carrying soulful, transcendental energy, both the sarangi and electric sitar contribute rich flavors to a delicately spicy whole. The beautiful vocal work of Prakash is featured on the meditative introductory “ Clear the Dust ” and “ The Blessing ”, where Lloyd evokes “ Tone Poem ” in his mystic chants. “ Jai Ganga ”, a traditional piece drawn from the group’s archives, is a vivid, celebratory marching dedication to the sacred Ganges river, while “ Tagore ”, featuring Lloyd on flute, is a premium Carnatic output with a lingering melody and mesmerizing rhythm, recorded live in Santa Barbara, CA, in 2014. In turn, “ Eternal Dreaming ”, using a sustained chord as a drone, reflects a meditative temperament. With the rhythm team put to excellent use throughout the recording, Sangam and Friends shares multicultural stories, keeping Lloyd’s distinct style front and center. items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家 Omar Sosa 在意大利 Fazioli 钢琴音乐厅完成了一次两小时的完全即兴录制，专辑由此原始素材经后期加入人声采样、打击乐、循环与田野录音等元素塑造成型。评论围绕专辑诞生的语境展开——疫情封锁、个人生活转折与厂牌合作邀约共同促成了这场创作。Sosa 本人阐述其创作哲学：拒绝被风格归类，强调第一遍录音的自然直觉与'少即是多'的美学，提倡融合多种影响的自由表达，并批判流媒体算法对音乐分类的简化。评论以《Inside the Spirit》开篇的演奏为分析切入点，描述了琴弦的延音共鸣、后期叠加的轻柔打击乐与电子音效的处理手法，呈现了一张融合古巴音乐根源、即兴自由爵士、当代古典钢琴语汇与电子声响设计的跨界作品。

items.body: Venetian maestro Gigi Masin, active since the early tape era, threads MIDI phrasing with soft techno patterns and submerged tonal layers. A sense of persistence rather than grief alone Gigi Masin returns with Movement, his first solo LP since Calypso, shifting ambient into pulse-driven structures and sequenced motion. Out on May 29th via Sacred Bones, Movement reframes ambient as physical music, built for shared space, where loops, low frequencies, and sustained tones guide the body as much as the ear. “Deception Dance” has been the first excerpt. This new album is significantly influenced by the recent collaboration with sound designer Rod Modell and also benefits from Anacleto Vitolo’s excellent mastering work. “UMI” and its minimalist style add a touch of coolness that doesn’t feel cold, transporting you to a chill corner of a sweaty room, the same space shared with the seven-and-a-half-minute “Deception Dance,” a minimal techno track that, with snippets of alien-sounding phrases. “Lost,” is dedicated to the disappearance of his wife: an act of love and tenderness conveyed through a synthesized trumpet, representing a “love letter that was no longer received and was thrown into the river.” The more rhythmic tracks (such as “Golden” or ) have been interpreted as a tribute/exploration that blends and reinterprets techno-funk sounds, Balearic bossa nova (in the vein of Manuel Göttsching), and classic Balearic influences. In 2007, the beloved Italian composer lost his entire musical archive in a house flood, forcing him to put music on the back burner for a while. These events could have disrupted his work entirely. Instead, Masin continued to create. The album reflects a sense of persistence rather than grief alone. There is emotion present, but it is expressed through subtle shifts rather than dramatic gestures. Movement is available on Sacred Bones. [Bandcamp] Movement by Gigi Masin  The post Gigi Masin :: Movement (Sacred Bones) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
items._cn_summary: 意大利电子音乐人Gigi Masin暌违多年推出新专辑《Movement》，将氛围音乐重新塑形为具有脉动结构的物理性音乐。专辑以循环、低频和持续音调引导身体律动，将氛围从静态聆听转向共享空间中的身体感知。曲目在极简techno框架中融入外星般的合成短语与Balearic bossa nova元素，Manuel Göttsching式的techno-funk脉络贯穿其中。献给亡妻的《Lost》以合成小号传递一封无法送达的情书，以克制取代悲恸。整张专辑体现了创作者在2007年洪水摧毁全部音乐档案后仍然坚持创作的韧性，情感表达通过微小变化而非戏剧性手法呈现，Rod Modell的合作与Anacleto Vitolo的母带处理为作品增色不少。

items.body: When I spoke with Bon Harris in February, on EBM Day of all days, our conversation kept returning to something more fundamental than legacy. Creativity. At one point, talking about what had changed across four decades of Nitzer Ebb and what had stubbornly remained, he said: “The thing that never changes is the desire to be creative.” He described it as an instinctive force, something present from the moment he wakes up in the morning. Today, 12 August, Bon Harris turns 61, and that sentence feels like a much better place to begin than another ceremonial list of influential records. Because although Harris is inseparable from Nitzer Ebb and from a particular idea of physical electronic music, his creative life has always been considerably wider than the role history assigned him. Born Vaughan David Harris in Chelmsford on 12 August 1965, he co-founded Nitzer Ebb in 1982 with school friends Douglas McCarthy, David Gooday and Simon Granger. The early records developed a brutally economical musical vocabulary: sequenced electronics, percussion, repetition, command-like vocals and a relationship with rhythm that treated the body as seriously as the intellect. After signing with Mute, “That Total Age” arrived in 1987, followed by “Belief”, “Showtime”, “Ebbhead” and “Big Hit”; after the long interruption, “Industrial Complex” followed in 2010. Harris’s role inside that history is difficult to reduce to “keyboard player.” His own Bon Harris biography describes him as a founder member and principal writer/producer of Nitzer Ebb, while his work has encompassed programming, synthesizers, percussion, vocals, composition and production. The machinery was important, obviously, but talking to him earlier this year reminded me how strongly his understanding of electronic music remains connected to physical presence. “Music historically is a communal pastime,” he told me. For Harris, the live show remains the highest expression of that idea: people gathering in one place, the performers giving energy to the audience and receiving it back. That philosophy explains quite a lot about Nitzer Ebb. The famous severity of the programming has always contained something deeply social: this is music designed to happen between bodies. But Bon did not stop exploring when Nitzer Ebb first went quiet. After relocating to Los Angeles, he moved further into studio production and composition, with scoring work becoming his primary source of income for several years. His work outside the band has included Billy Corgan and The Smashing Pumpkins, Marilyn Manson and Avril Lavigne, while working with arranger Andrew Poppy during Nitzer Ebb had already given him an early view into orchestration and scoring. His film and television work later included music for Project Runway, Top Chef and NBC’s Treasure Hunters. There was also Maven, the post-Nitzer Ebb project he was already developing by the late 1990s, which placed Bon much further forward as a vocalist. Years later, BLACK LINE offered almost the inverse experience of his traditional role in Nitzer Ebb: a deliberately collaborative environment in which he could enter music already being shaped by other people, find his own space inside it and, as he put it, feel like one of the band rather than having the musical architecture resting largely on his shoulders. Then there is bonharris:arts, the platform Bon created for work extending beyond Nitzer Ebb into his own music, animation and collaborations. During the 2020 lockdown, “songs:from the lemon tree” began as a series of intimate performances filmed in his Los Angeles garden, with Bon radically rearranging songs that had been important to his own musical development. The project also brought him back to sustained lead vocals after the Maven period. If “songs the lemon tree” exposed one side of Harris, “mikro” opened another. Released as his first substantial solo project in almost two decades, it joined raw modular synthesis with the funk, soul and R&B that surrounded his childhood and adolescence. Harris described the idea as “twenty-first-century electronic punk funk“; the recordings brought electronic programming into contact with brass, vocals and a rhythmic vocabulary very different from the disciplined severity people automatically associate with Nitzer Ebb. And Bon Harris extends beyond sound. Harris has spoken about teaching himself animation after suffering music-industry burnout, finding in it another creative language when he needed some distance from music production. He has also discussed ambitions to combine animation and music in larger narrative or theatrical forms. It is an interesting detail because it makes his career look less like a sequence of side projects and more like a restless investigation of how an idea can be given form: through rhythm, voice, image, movement, performance or technology. That question feels particularly poignant in 2026. Douglas McCarthy died in June 2025, and Harris has since carried a much greater vocal responsibility in Nitzer Ebb while continuing the band with David Gooday, Simon Granger and the wider live unit. When we spoke in February, he was candid about the difficulty of that transition. Singing Douglas’s words every night had forced him to enter those lyrics at a depth he had never needed to before; he spoke about being repeatedly reminded of what an extraordinary lyricist and singular vocalist his friend had been. Yet he was equally insistent that Nitzer Ebb was not simply becoming a memorial. In February, Harris confirmed that a new album had been written and was awaiting the administrative work necessary for release. He said there were roughly 15 or 16 finished pieces from which the final album would be selected, including recordings featuring McCarthy as well as newer material written and sung by Harris. His description was telling: the album should carry one period forward while opening another. No later confirmed release date has been announced that I could verify at the time of writing, while Nitzer Ebb remain active onstage, with another US run scheduled to begin later in August. There was another answer from that February conversation that stayed with me. When I asked what he hoped people would eventually remember about Nitzer Ebb, Harris did not choose the sound, the influence or even the extraordinary physical force of the concerts. He chose commitment. He talked about the financial, emotional and spiritual difficulty of sustaining a creative life, about encountering people who do not understand what you are doing, and about continuing anyway. What mattered to him was that Nitzer Ebb had remained committed to its own artistic vision and had refused to back away from the work. That seems like the right thing to celebrate today. There is the Bon Harris who helped create one of electronic music’s most recognizable rhythmic languages. There is the producer, programmer and synthesist. The drummer and increasingly prominent singer. The studio collaborator and screen composer. The man who returned to the songs that formed him and rebuilt them under a lemon tree. The modular-funk experimenter. The animator. And there is still the person getting up in the morning with ideas that need somewhere to go. At 61, the history is substantial. Fortunately, Bon Harris still seems much more interested in creating than in becoming history. Happy birthday, Bon. About Bon Harris and Nitzer Ebb Nitzer Ebb formed in Chelmsford, Essex in 1982, when Bon Harris co-founded the group with school friends Douglas McCarthy, David Gooday and Simon Granger. Signed to Mute Records, the band built a stark, body-driven strand of EBM around sequenced electronics, percussion and command-like vocals, releasing its debut album, “That Total Age”, in 1987. “Belief” followed in 1989, “Showtime” in 1990, “Ebbhead” in 1991 and “Big Hit” in 1995, after which the band went on extended hiatus. Nitzer Ebb reconvened in the mid-2000s and released “Industrial Complex” in 2010, and has continued to tour internationally in the years since, with Gooday and Granger rejoining the live lineup alongside Harris and McCarthy. Douglas McCarthy died in June 2025, and Harris has since led Nitzer Ebb as its vocalist as well as its programmer and instrumentalist, continuing the band’s live schedule into 2026 while completing a new studio album.
items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评以Bon Harris六十一岁生日为切入点，回顾了他与Nitzer Ebb自1982年以来的创作历程。乐队以序列电子、重复节拍与命令式人声构建了一种极简而具有身体性的音乐语言，涵盖了《That Total Age》《Belief》《Showtime》《Ebbhead》《Big Hit》以及2010年的《Industrial Complex》。Harris本人不仅是键盘手，更横跨编程、合成器、打击乐、人声、作曲与制作多个领域。文章着重讨论了他对电子音乐的理解——将现场演出视为音乐的最高表达形式，强调音乐发生在身体之间的社会性。在Nitzer Ebb沉寂期间，他转向好莱坞影视配乐与制作工作，参与了Billy Corgan、Marilyn Manson、Avril Lavigne等艺人项目，并涉足电视音乐领域。文章还提到了他与Andrew Poppy的合作以及后Nitzer Ebb时期的Maven项目，展现了一位工业电子先驱在主乐队之外的多面向创作轨迹。

items.body: Based in Gothenburg, SYNVILLA treats music and moving images as organs within the same unruly body. Heavy experimental rock, psychedelia, post-punk, and noise meet video art that is seductive, threatening, and frequently difficult to separate from the performance itself. Riffs drag and buckle, rhythms take crooked routes, and warped melodies push through distortion with a streak of playful menace. During their live performances, SYNVILLA uses projected video as part of the stage presentation. While the band plays, footage of bodies and faces repeats, divides, and distorts across the screen, changing in step with the music. The projections give the audience a visual extension of the songs and place video art at the center of the concert experience. SYNVILLA return with their latest single, Milky Breath, released through Beans on Toast Records. The song accompanies the announcement of the forthcoming GRINDMOTHER EP. Thick drums give Milky Breath a heavy, deliberate gait. Psychedelic guitars slither around them in warped curves, while a buzzing low register carries the chest-deep vibration of a didgeridoo. Above this mass, the vocals quiver with witchy poise, stretching each phrase somewhere between a warning, an invitation, and an involuntary exhalation. The arrangement gains force through repetition as its parts return slightly damaged, bend out of shape, and eventually break into a physical act of release. SYNVILLA describes the song as a surrender of conscious control, with social masks falling away as bodily impulse assumes command. The title intensifies that tension: milk suggests nourishment and breath signals life, yet the two words together feel thick, close, and almost claustrophobic. Resistance registers as muscle memory, the body shaking loose the instructions it has learned to obey. Few smiles in recent memory have looked as hungry as the one occupying the Milky Breath video. A black-clad figure appears beneath two enormous horn-like forms while its mouth stretches into a crowded, impossible crescent, recalling the Mouth of Sauron in Peter Jackson’s The Return of the King. The eyes vanish, the head divides, and the grin remains fixed, as though it has taken possession of the person wearing it. Victor Cornelius turns that premise into five and a half minutes of analog-video mutation. Solarized pinks, acidic orange, and cyan pass over faces and anatomical forms. The central figure is duplicated into contact sheets, folded into bilateral symmetry, pressed behind mesh, and expanded into a featureless white oval. Banks of lidless eyes crowd the frame while faces swim beneath watery tracking errors, hands skitter across a doubled torso, and human figures collapse into stark silhouettes. Throughout these transformations, the enormous grin functions as a gruesome visual refrain. It survives every attempt to erase the face around it, repeatedly returning with its wet rows of teeth intact. By the final passage, the video resembles a late-night television transmission seized by an intelligence that has only recently learned the mechanics of a human smile. Watch the video for Milky Breath below: With two albums behind them, SYNVILLA celebrated their latest release, Feberfoster, with a sold-out concert at Skeppet GBG. The collective has shared stages with Hällas, Skraeckoedlan, and MaidaVale, while appearing at festivals including Fuzztival, Muskelrock, and Sonic Ritual. Milky Breath is out now through Beans on Toast Records. The forthcoming GRINDMOTHER EP will follow, with its release date to be announced. items._cn_summary: 瑞典哥德堡实验集体SYNVILLE将音乐与动态影像视为同一有机体的器官，重型实验摇滚、迷幻、后朋克与噪音在视觉投影的延伸中融为一体。新单曲《Milky Breath》以厚重的鼓点铺设沉重的步态，迷幻吉他以扭曲曲线蜿蜒其上，低频嗡鸣模拟迪吉里杜的胸腔振动，人声在警告、邀请与无意识呼气之间摇摆。歌曲通过重复积累力量，各部件以轻微损伤的状态回归，最终在身体的释放中崩裂。MV由Victor Cornelius执导，五分半钟的模拟视频变异将面孔分裂、对称折叠、网格压缩，无嘴之眼成群涌现，而那个巨大的笑容作为视觉叠句贯穿始终，在每一次抹除中顽固回归。

items.body:
Reissue of the debut by A.G. Cook & Danny L Harle’s earliest duo, Dux Content, initially dispensed on Gamsonite, a predecessor of P.C. Music, and teasing out strands of makina, electro-house, bardcore and trap with combo’s of ludic, recombinant suss & sharp sound design that became their calling card.

Scrolling back to what now feels like a distant world - the up-for-grabs edges of early 2010s - ‘Lifestyle’ maps out formative aspects of the two producers, still relatively fresh from music studies at Goldsmiths, and making their mark in a burgeoning “internet music” scene. Of course they’re both now chart-topping songwriters/producers with credits for Charli xcx, Dua Lipa, Oklou, et al, but here they’re positively bubbling over with wild, yet disciplined, fusions of upfront hard dance with jazz, contemporary classical and pop that, with the benefit of hindsight, place them in a contemporaneous cultural slipstream with likes of Cracksmurf/T C F or James Ferraro, and soon-to-be spar, SOPHIE.

‘Lifestyle’ is the sound of two minds scything thru cultures and sounds they grew up with - Harle coming from a family background spanning his Geordie dad, John Harle’s BBC scores and early taste for makina’s stacked melodies - and bonding over a shared love of Captain Beefheart, Archie Sheep, and Tim & Eric, all evident in their grasp of shiny, commercial hooks and complex rhythm wrapped up with daft grin and wink. Shake a wand anywhere and you’ll hit a mad one, from the crazed midi piano house of ‘Voice of an Angel’, thru the jazz-fink of ‘City Break’ and ‘Hero Next Door’, free wheeling jazz trance of ‘Heart of Death’ and pitch bent panpipes of ‘Business Class’.
items._genre: electro-house / hard dance / makina / electronic fusion / pop experimental
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是A.G. Cook与Danny L Harle早期二人组Dux Content的首张作品再版，发行于PC Music前身厂牌Gamsonite。两位制作人当时刚从伦敦大学金匠学院毕业，处于2010年代初互联网音乐的萌芽期。专辑将硬核舞曲与爵士、当代古典、流行乐进行融合，呈现出大胆但有节制的实验性。Harle的成长背景为他带来了makina堆叠旋律的基因与古典音乐的训练，两人共同沉迷于Captain Beefheart、Archie Shepp以及Tim & Eric的怪趣味美学。作品中既有疯狂midi钢琴house的《Voice of an Angel》，爵士小品的《City Break》《Hero Next Door》，自由的爵士trance《Heart of Death》，以及弯音排箫的《Business Class》，体现了两位创作者在多元文化声音中穿行的早期面貌。

items.body:
The Mitteleuropa enigma is strong on the 2nd original LP by Pablo’s Eye for Stroom, commanding attention to noctilucent, cinematic synth scapes laced with hand-played drums and poetry that plays out like a waking dream.

Active since ’89, the rotating assembly of Pablo’s Eye, headed by Axel Libeert, have plotted a unique course thru the backwaters of art rock, ambient, fantasy soundtrack music, and whatever else they fancy, leading to a pair of retrospectives on Stroom in 2018-19, plus the cult EP ‘Bardo For Pablo’, and fresh material on ‘The Light Was Sharp, Our Eyes Were Closed’ (2024).

Here represented by Marie Mandi, Luc Laret, Thierry Royo, Richard Skinner, Axel Libeert, and Ludwig Lapauw on ‘Everything You Give Away’, they follow noses for a typically low slung and resoundingly atmospheric album primed to seduce anyone in its path, as they stealthily proceed from the nightfall of ‘Walking the Line’, reminding us of DAAC, to the blushed choral pads and trip hop bass of ‘Reverie’ and Reese bass-gilded centrepiece ‘A dash of raspberry’, and ultimately the widescreen departure of ‘October ’75’. 

Trés classy.
items._genre: ambient / cinematic synth / art rock / atmospheric
items._cn_summary: 比利时音乐人 Axel Libeert 领导的 Pablo's Eye 发行第二张全长专辑《Everything You Give Away》，由 Stroom 厂牌推出。乐评指出作品延续了中欧艺术摇滚的独特路径，将夜光般的电影化合成器音景、手工演奏的鼓点与诗歌朗诵交织，营造出近似清醒之梦的氛围。六位音乐人参与录制，曲目从夜色笼罩的开篇过渡到合唱铺底的朦胧段落，最终在宽银幕式的尾声处升腾。整张专辑走低姿态路线，层次丰富、气息绵长，被评价为极具品位的氛围佳作，与 DAAC 等前辈的余韵遥相呼应。

items.body:
Mu-inspired space cadets KiF Productions livicate their play of Japanese environmental ambient electronics, Hassellian 4th world, the KLF’s ‘Chill Out’, and Eno-esque harmonic perfumes, to the dearly departed Keith McIvor​.

"Passiflora (Passifloraceae) is a genus of around 550 species of flowering plants, native to the tropical and subtropical Americas. The Passion Flower is a plant of improbable beauty - its blooms almost too intricate to be real, its climbing habit a quiet kind of determination. It has been used for centuries as a remedy for anxiety and sleeplessness, something that slows us and the world around us down.

Fresh from last year's triumphant debut by KiF; Still Out, Passiflora, the album, follows the plant from its very beginning. It opens in darkness - 'Secret of the Seed', dormant, waiting - before the first tentative stir of 'First Movement' and the long, instinctive reach of 'Seeking Light'. From there, the journey unfolds with the patience of something that has no choice but to grow: drinking, climbing, flowering. 'Song of the Vine' carries the plant's quiet insistence upward, while 'Florescence' and 'Pollination Dream' catch it at its most open - that brief, extraordinary moment of full bloom. Then the turn. 'Fruiting (Slight Return)' and finally 'Return to Earth' - the cycle completing itself, giving back what it always borrowed.

Each track is a stage. The whole is a life cycle."
items._genre: ambient / fourth world / environmental electronics / drone
items._cn_summary: KiF Productions 的《Passiflora》是一张以植物生命周期为结构蓝本的专辑，从黑暗中的种子萌发，经由藤蔓攀爬、花朵盛开，直至果熟归土，每一曲目对应自然生长的一个阶段。音乐融合了日本环境氛围电子、哈塞尔式的第四世界冥想、The KLF《Chill Out》的悠闲律动以及Eno式和声处理，形成缓慢展开的音景。作为献给小卡带机器创始成员Keith McIvor的纪念作品，专辑以概念叙事取代传统曲目排列，将声音设计、生物隐喻与冥想气质融为一体，呈现出兼具植物学严谨性与声音实验性的听觉旅程。

items.body:
Ambient composer Natalia Beylis leads an ensemble of Nyahh’s finest in her landscape-shaped evocation of a field in Leitrim, Éire, quietly meditating on the natural logic of birds and trees.

‘Around Here The Birds Plant The Trees’ is Beylis’ slow-burn, long-form arrangement for quintet - Eimear Reidy (cello), Tola Custy (fiddle), Ailbhe Nic Oireachtaigh & Ultan O’Brien (violin), and Willie Stewart (percussion) - seeded in her reading of a blackbird’s dawn chorus, and subsequent conversation with a local farmer on how “birds are the architects of the living landscape”. It follows some 40 solo albums over the past 20 years (not to mention jams with Woven Skull and Tomuttontu) with a considered approach to what lies just beyond her home; typically drawing on her attentive reading of the rural soundsphere to transmute the poetry of birdsong and the natural world into expressive musical metaphor.

The low bowed cello tone of regular spar Eimear Reidy underlines and opens out a breezy space where where the fiddle and violinists criss-cross air in reserved melodic flight and plucky figures that alternate like the play of light on Ireland’s remote North West. The piece unfolds to boggy pockets of percussion and passages of barely-there, hushed gloam, as though the wind itself was generating the players’ gestures, which rise to cloud castle hover around the midway, only to depart for Nyahh label boss Willie Stewart’s rolling drum thunder and scrape of Ailbhe Nic Oireachtaigh's fiddle rooted in the rolling landscape. Ultimately the folk soul of the turf rises in its final section, resembling a rousing, swaying folk song voiced by the strings in ideally creaky discord.
items._cn_summary: 娜塔莉亚·贝利斯以爱尔兰北部莱特里姆的田野景观为灵感，创作了这部长篇五重奏作品。专辑构思源自一只黑莺的黎明合唱，以及与当地农民关于鸟类如何塑造自然景观的对话。整首作品以低沉的大提琴音色开篇，逐步展开弦乐与提琴的克制对话，间或穿插打击乐的低沉吟唱。中段乐章逐渐隆起，弦乐声部凝聚成悬浮的音云，随后过渡到爱尔兰民间舞曲般的节奏脉动。作品将这些弦乐与打击乐手置于一个由鸟鸣、田野风声与自然诗意所激发的空间之中，呈现出介于环境音乐、当代古典与爱尔兰民谣之间的模糊地带，以听觉的方式描绘了爱尔兰西北部荒野中那片土地的声音逻辑。

items.body:
Cloud-seeding dub techno sorcery x Rhythm & Sound worship by Stephen Hitchell’s cult cv313 and Radius projects, recorded in the heart of Detroit and preserved for posterity by Pole’s faithful remasters at Scape Berlin.

Echospace co-pilot Stephen Hitchell mans the cockpit solo on six sterling examples of Motor City dub techno purism within the 1st volume of ‘Altering Illusions’. His hallucinatory, synaesthetic tekkerz are in palpable effect from the damp bass thru to its noctilucent synth haze, bathing bodies in blissed-out arrangements that unfold up to 20 minutes in length, as with the echoes of BC’s ‘radiance’ registered in expansive parting piece ‘standing still’, and dredged up from drizzly depths on the cv313 rewire of Radius’ ‘Interpolation Tapes’.

Clubs are in the rearview for an 80 min trip deep under the hood of Echospace’s classic sound, fathoming deepest levels of sunken subs and elemental attrition on ‘i s i s’, and hingeing on Rhythm & Sound’s skankers' templates in ‘hypnosphere’ and mesmerising metallic resonance of ‘irradiate’, while ‘above clouds’ rises above the weather system into clearer, blue-skied dub techno lushness; think post-storm Lake Erie panoramas diffused by Wolfgang Voigt’s GAS.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Stephen Hitchell以cv313名义在底特律录制的dub techno作品集，经Pole所在的Scape厂牌重新母带处理后再度发行。Hitchell延续了Echospace项目标志性的深沉低频与朦胧合成器美学，六首曲目时长可达二十分钟，强调空间的延展与声音的缓慢演化。作品明显受Rhythm & Sound模板影响，低音线如水下涌动，合成器织体呈现出雾状扩散感，末曲呼应BC系ambient的悠远意境。部分段落以极简的金属共鸣和深沉潜艇般的次低频构成，营造出脱离俱乐部语境的冥想氛围；另一部分则抬升至云层之上，进入GAS式开阔音景。整体是面向深度聆听者的环境向电子乐再版，强调底特律dub techno传统中安静、缓慢、沉浸的一脉。

items.body:
Chicago’s excellent, shapeshifting Kino Disk chase 8004’s ace dub abstractions with Eustress’ actions in familiar meadows of overgrown FX, farming post-dub techno landscapes highly tipped FFO Vladislav Delay, Echospace, False Aralia.

Peripheral to the Windy City’s fecund undergrowth, Indianapolis-based Heath Gillespie aka Eustress practises forms of dub techno at gauzy arm’s reach from the OG source. On the six tracks of ‘Exit’, his 2nd release for the label, he distorts familiar tropes to taste, diffusing a palette of windswept dub chords and unanchored bass in space crackling with an iridescent grayscale filament. 

His approach broadly swerves dub techno’s club momentum in favour of soothing meditation, letting everything hang out and slosh, loosely suspended in gritty yet lush amniotic plasm with an effect calling to mind the etheric depths of Echospace or even Werkbund’s atmospheric enigmas.

A hands-on background as mixing engineer comes to the fore in his work’s sensory tactility, convecting minds from a slow tempest to beatific bliss-out, rumbles of distant dub chord thunder and carpet rolling gouch-out, ultimately stranding up on the 8 min peninsula of ‘Exit 6’, under a borealis play of smudged, harmonised light, nerves combed into the breeze.
items._cn_summary: 这是印第安纳波利斯制作人Eustress在芝加哥厂牌Kino Disk发行的第二张专辑，包含六首曲目。整张作品有意回避dub techno典型的俱乐部节奏动能，转向冥想式氛围构建，将飘渺的dub和弦与无锚bass音色散布在充满灰度光泽的声场空间中。制作人作为混音工程师的背景使作品具有强烈的感官触感，声音在粗粝而丰沛的质感中缓缓流动。从开场缓慢的风暴逐渐过渡到宁静的迷醉状态，远处dub和弦的雷鸣与地毯般的质感层叠交织。终曲长达八分钟，在模糊的极光般和声光影中收束，整体呈现出一种漂浮于液态介质中的沉浸式听觉体验。
