items.body: REWORK have been around long enough to know that club music’s supposedly clean breaks with the past are usually rather messier affairs. Michael Kübler and Daniel Varga formed the Stuttgart electronic project in 2000 with French vocalist Laetitia Rometsch, releasing their first EP, Anyway I Know You, through Frankfurt’s Playhouse Records. Their 2003 debut album, Fall Right Now, brought together early cuts, including “You’re So Just Just,” and established the combination they would come to describe as “new wave house”: spare machines, clipped funk, European pop instincts, and vocals that regard seduction as a form of mild antagonism. Later records for Playhouse, Visionquest, Get Physical, and their own Exlove imprint continued to complicate the boundaries between house, techno, electro, and pop at a time when those distinctions still carried considerable tribal weight. Released through Exlove Records on July 17th, the three-track Disco Love Remixes EP returns to the title track of REWORK’s March 2025 release. The original followed 2024’s Never Again and a Get Physical release that paired REWORK’s updated version of “You’re So Just Just” with separate remixes by Cinthie and Seth Troxler with Ryan Crosson. The new collection brings together interpretations by Neu-Romancer and Jennifer Touch alongside REWORK’s own “Disco Love2,” a special edit that reaches back toward the economical architecture of their Playhouse years. Sira Kübler’s vocal gives “Disco Love” its human temperature, sitting against bass and percussion disciplined enough to make each small adjustment feel consequential. The Playhouse influence is explicit in “Disco Love2,” although the track avoids becoming an exercise in period reconstruction. Its disco vocabulary has been pared down until glamour becomes something harder, stranger and slightly severe. Neu-Romancer is the solo project of Laura Bailey, an Australian musician, producer and DJ originally from Fremantle and now based in Berlin. Her 2023 debut EP, Neue Romantika, appeared on Zanias’ Fleisch Records, drawing on Italo disco, darkwave, EBM, and New Romantic references across four original tracks and a Zanias remix. The record included “Remnants,” a collaboration with Kris Baha, while Bailey’s broader history includes playing bass with goth outfit VV & The Void and punk band CIERN, as well as performing in Zanias’ live group. Her connection with REWORK predates the present remix: the artists released the two-track Call You Up EP together in June 2025. For “Disco Love,” Neu-Romancer takes the material into a more insistent space. Her remix thickens the rhythmic motion and introduces a bouncing, almost predatory momentum, making the track feel as if it were designed for the point in a club night when conversation has ceased to be useful. Details accumulate without clutter, and the arrangement maintains a peculiar forward pressure even as its gestures become more expansive. Neu-Romancer Jennifer Touch is a Berlin-based producer, singer, live musician and DJ whose work draws in part on her upbringing in eastern Germany. After issuing her first solo record in 2014, she developed a body of work that moves freely between post-punk, industrial electronics, wave music and club production. Her albums Behind the Wall and Midnight Proposals appeared through FatCat Records in 2020 and 2023, respectively, followed by Aging at Airports through Fabrika Records in September 2025. She has also released music through Riotvan, Eskimo Recordings, and Live at Robert Johnson, and has collaborated with Curses and Paranoid London. Touch approaches “Disco Love” from another angle, bringing greater emotional abrasion to its polished frame. Her version pairs cold-wave textures with a forceful club structure, allowing tension to build around Sira Kübler’s vocals and the regimented percussion. The bass bears down with greater weight while the upper register remains brittle and exposed. It is an effective reminder of how closely post-punk’s severity and dance music’s physicality have always sat beside one another. Jennifer Touch That relationship between post-punk and dance music also explains the logic behind Exlove Records, REWORK’s own imprint. Its catalog moves between synthpop, house, techno, electro, post-punk and synthwave without treating genre boundaries as border control, with releases from REWORK alongside She Lies, Philipp Roller, Sugartin and A Youth. Across more than two decades, REWORK’s tracks have also been handed to Andrew Weatherall, Roman Flügel, Trentemøller, Magda, Paranoid London, Cinthie and Seth Troxler for reinterpretation. They have little need to prove their underground credentials. “Disco Love” sounds more interested in what can still be done with them. Listen to Disco Love Remixes below and order the EP here. items.body: Summer songs traditionally have an unfair advantage. They get cars with the windows down, imprudent decisions, swimming pools, romances improved by temporary geography. Soft Vein’s new single Another Summer seems suspicious of all that. Justin Chamberlain approaches the season as someone might regard an old photograph found in a drawer: with affection, perhaps, but also with the knowledge that whatever happened there has already escaped its participants. The title suggests recurrence, but Chamberlain sounds interested in what recurrence fails to restore. Another season comes around. The people inhabiting it have changed. The song, the final single from Soft Vein’s forthcoming All We’ve Known of Heaven, has some of the suave composure of Robert Palmer and the eccentric pop intelligence of John Foxx and Peter Gabriel. A rounded bass line moves beneath clipped vocal phrases and lush synthesizers, which periodically rise around Chamberlain without swallowing him. The staccato chant and hook are especially good, giving an otherwise sumptuous ballad a curious nervousness, as though somebody has prepared the perfect sentence and then discovered that speaking it aloud changes its meaning. This year, Soft Vein has moved further toward synthpop, although Chamberlain retains a detached, cerebral chill. Another Summer may be the most persuasive argument yet for that development: a beautiful arrangement can make emotional confusion more acute. The bass has an almost tactile roundness; the keyboards occasionally widen into luminous sheets; his voice stays exposed in the middle, stylish without becoming mannered. Every element appears to know exactly how much room it should occupy. Chamberlain sings softly, often close enough to conversational volume that his restraint becomes part of the song’s psychology. Soft Vein has always been interested in the humiliations of wanting something from another person: reassurance, sex, permanence, an explanation. Another Summer finds him contemplating communication; his delivery has the attractive uncertainty of a person willing to disclose something before deciding whether disclosure was wise. That divided temperament has followed Soft Vein from 2023’s Pressed in Glass through Through Blinds, the 2024 record that brought Chamberlain’s songwriting into sharper focus. The 2025 EP From Another Room, featuring remixes by Twin Tribes and Qual alongside covers of formative artists, offered a useful bridge. All We’ve Known of Heaven is now available for preorder ahead of its release through Artoffact Records. Soft Vein will mark the album with a September 11 Los Angeles release show at Zebulon, presented by Minty Boi, with Catherine Moan as direct support and Secret Attraction opening. Buy tickets here. items.body: Across the vast American sprawl, post-punk and darkwave have taken root in cities throughout the country, with each local scene giving the music its own character. Among the rising bands within that wider movement, Casket Cassette and Stare Away represent two distant geographic poles: Los Angeles and New York City, the City of Angels and Gotham, relentless sunshine and after-dark intensity. This summer, the bands have closed nearly 3,000 miles of continental distance on Casket Cassette’s Reducer Tour, the Los Angeles project’s first headlining run. Constant Laval Williams and Ben Nelson first became friends when Stare Away joined a Casket Cassette bill at Sip Studios in Jersey City, where they discovered common ground in Joy Division’s rhythmic force and Ian Curtis’s songwriting, as well as recovery, poetry, and the desire to exorcise personal damage through catharsis of a crowd. Both artists entered the tour with their most substantial releases to date. Casket Cassette’s third album, Reducer, released June 12, turns experiences of erasure, constriction, recovery, and the aftermath of the Los Angeles fires into a ten-song study of what survives when a life and community have been pared back. Post-Punk.com followed the record’s development through Kiss Me Awake and Show Me a Sign, songs that brought Williams’s doomed romanticism into sharper electronic relief. On July 31, Stare Away released its seven-song debut, In Absence, via à La Carte Records, drawing on Nelson’s seclusion after sobriety, the depths of addiction, and relationships that continued to exert their pull. Its closing track, Familiar, gave those concerns one of the album’s most immediate expressions. Onstage, their geographical and musical differences sharpen the pairing. Casket Cassette channels the strange darkness that flourishes beneath Los Angeles sunshine through electronic pressure and doomed pop melody, while Stare Away draws on Gotham’s nocturnal velocity with tensile bass, urgent guitar, and the close physical charge of an early post-punk club. As the tour enters its final stretch, Post-Punk.com spoke with Williams and Nelson about the records that guided Reducer and In Absence, the friendship behind the tour, the cultures of their respective cities, and the collaboration already waiting beyond the final date: Ben, in absence, feels like a reference to the terms “In Memoriam” or “To Absent Friends”. What kind of absence does the title refer to, and what emotional or thematic thread holds the album together? The record is a massive reflection on the past couple years of my life. I definitely secluded myself from a lot of aspects of living in New York City so I could just focus and make progress on better finding myself after getting sober. I just disappeared for a while from going out and was working full-time at a job I absolutely hated. I looked at myself & how insane the state of the world currently is, and put everything into my craft to reflect my own mysteries, questions & realizations of isolation, depths of addiction, and relationships I’ve had that were very important to me. I think when you put your heart into something physical and artistic, people will truly relate rather than follow like a cheap social media posting scheme and will feel much more fruitful and fulfilling in the end. I feel like I discovered more about myself throughout the process of writing this record than I ever would if I hadn’t. The title track sums up the entire record and each following track dissects it in its own way musically and lyrically. Sitting with Mike Morello in the studio and putting so much time and emotion into each song really tied it all up with a bow. Ben, which artists, records, or musical periods were foremost in your mind while making In Absence? Or writers and filmmakers perhaps? To really narrow it down, New Order’s “Movement” demos and writing sessions, The Cure’s “Faith” home demos, and The Sound’s “Jeopardy” record are in my everyday rotation. When it came down to pure influence, I really wanted to write from a direction as a band involved in the first wave with a maturing mid-80s attitude. The sculpting behind what defined an emerging underground genre is what I’ll always strive for when writing. Experimental films and beatnik writers of the late 50s and 60s called me to think more of vulnerability in expression when it came down to writing the lyrics. Ben, was there one song that unlocked the direction of In Absence and helped you understand what the rest of the record needed to become? “I Can’t Escape Myself” by the Sound. Truly a masterpiece of a track in my opinion. The daily hysteria of living life on life’s terms regardless of situation or control over one’s ability to have an answer for everything that shapes our identities and emotions is kind of a beauty in a sense, which makes us all unique in our own ways. The album art shot by Julie Lodhy really captured that reflection literally. Constant, what first set Reducer in motion, and how did the album develop from that initial idea into the finished record? I’d been spending most of my time focusing on crafting standout singles (Bouquet, Broken Tomorrow, etc.), and I wanted to return to another cohesive project. Specifically, for album #3, I wanted to respond to the erasure, reduction, and alienation I’d been feeling after returning home to LA from graduate school at the Iowa Writers’ Workshop, and in the wake of the LA fires. In a short period of time, my community of friends and my childhood home had both burned, shrunk, or vanished. It was a period of interpersonal, mental, and physical loss. I first explored these themes in the context of inward reflection, and then expanded into an examination of my past and my relationship to others. I also chose to incorporate increasingly poetic elements (such as references to Robert Lowell’s Skunk Hour in Kiss Me Awake, a poem in the interlude, and various lyrics that leaned more deeply into nuanced metaphor). The instruments ended up expressing rage, loss, and existential claustrophobia via the use of heavy basslines and aggressive drums, coupled with ethereal anthemic synths and the occasional heartfelt guitar line. What made me fall in love with the darkwave and post-punk genres to begin with was their ability to honestly express pain and darkness while also transfiguring that same pain into something beautiful and danceable. I can only hope this new album achieved that same duality. Constant, the word “reducer” suggests compression, subtraction, or stripping something to its essential form. What does the title mean to you, and how does it relate to the album’s songs? I think that you summed it up nicely. Like the choke-chain collar in the cover art, the title reflects a feeling of constriction (a minimization of self, community and environment). If you have the kind of brain that I have, life can sometimes feel like a series of “reductions” almost like pruning a bonsai tree to try to stay “right sized.” This has always been the case for me (especially as someone in recovery), but to have those reductions unwillingly extend into the world around me was intense. I think the songs all mirror this differently. I tried to let them be eclectic; sometimes disparate elements in conversation with one another are more comprehensive than similar elements. On songs like Kiss Me Awake and Melting Angels, there’s a wide-open purgatorial feeling that’s at odds with poignant, pared-down lyrics. A song like Pacific Coast Highway (PTSD) is a bittersweet memory, a bleeding echo of a whole. Show Me a Sign and Becoming burst past constriction into raw expressions of existential energy (etc.). Harmoniously, the album was mixed by Matia Simovich at Infinite Power Studios, who works almost exclusively with analog equipment. The process of mixing with analog machines is also a reduction of the nebulous revisions and additions of modern DAWs; when effects were baked into the stems, they were made singular and permanent. The same is true for Matia’s raw, minimalistic approach to tracking vocals on songs I recorded in-studio such as Becoming. The stems of some songs like Elegy were compressed together onto tape, and then re-digitized. Constant, which artists and records exerted the strongest influence on Reducer, and where can you hear those influences entering the album? There is always a plethora of artists within (and outside of) the genre influencing me. These, of course, include the giants whose footsteps we walk in (ie. Joy Division, The Cure, Bauhaus, Siouxsie, etc.) as well as the peers I have walking beside me (check out my Spotify playlist for reference). If I had to narrow it down for this specific album, I’d say: Charlotte Sometimes by The Cure, But Not Tonight by Depeche Mode (specifically the intro), the body of work by Sad Madona (who I’ve done two collaborations with (including on Reducer), and who I’ve been hanging out with when I visit the EU), the music of my buddy Jamison (aka Gossip Cult), indie and indie-adjacent bands I used to listen to when I was a kid (like Beach Fossils, Surf Curse, The Drums, etc,), The Smiths, Atmosphere by Joy Division, Crystal Castles, experimental acid/trance/house music I used to dance to at illegal warehouse raves downtown, Nitzer Ebb, Pagliacci by Leoncavallo, and various movie soundtracks. As a result, songs like Pacific Coast Highway (PTSD) blend post-punk and indie/alternative, while songs like Show Me a Sign or Apathy are darkwave with elements of electronica and EBM. All of these influences have allowed me to move in a new direction while staying true to my voice. Constant, you are also a poet, photographer, and filmmaker. How did those other disciplines shape the lyrics, imagery, or structure of Reducer? For me, all these disciplines come from the same source but are expressed in different ways, each appropriate for different moments/needs. They all allow us as human beings to try to source meaning from existence and our universe; a meaning we will never fully reach, but a beautiful process regardless. Photography and film rely on choice of subject and composition to craft visual narrative or provoke thought, while music relies on a similar, auditory gut-instinct. These instincts are also involved in poetry, but the act of writing and editing a poem requires a more microscopic cartography; everything must belong, every word must connect, every image must work against or for the conceit of the poem. Poetry is my first love. I’m obsessed with it. There’s a beautiful anarchy to it, yet an intentionality that I don’t find to be fully true in music or photography. Sometimes my lyrics are hyper poetic, and sometimes I want a break from the intense scrutiny required of poetry. Sometimes I just want to write an immediately understandable or quasi-cliché lyric for the catharsis of that immediacy; just want to say “I love you” or “I miss you” and not “your shadow lingers in the wake of my delinquent dreams.” Coming out of the Writers’ Workshop and being in the process of finishing my debut collection of poetry, poetry played a much larger role in this album than in the past. As I previously mentioned, there is a full poem in the Interlude; songs like Elegy and Kiss Me Awake both use rhyme schemes (or non-rhyming free-verse) in their lyrics and poetic imagery that is a new frontier for the fusion of poetry and music for me. I have a very vivid imagination; it can be very cinematic at times. I daydream a lot. When I was writing Reducer, photography and cinematography also informed the songs for sure—if I can’t imagine a visual narrative in my head while listening back to a song, then it’s probably not a good song. Structurally, I always want my albums to have a narrative arc as well. In the case of Reducer, I wanted to start with a feeling of stasis and constriction that then erupted into defiant forward movement. Constant and Ben, how did the two of you first meet, and what were your initial impressions of one another, both personally and as musicians? Ben: We met at the Jersey City date of his first US tour with Blood Club and dustbowlchampion at Sip Studios, it was so cool to be able to meet from being on complete opposite sides of the country, everyone was so inviting and kind and it was awesome being able to appreciate each others music. It was like going to a new school and kicking it off with another kid in class with similar interests. Constant: Ben and I met a few years ago on my first-ever national tour with Blood Club and Dustbowlchampion. I had already been aware of Ben’s music after finding it online and would religiously listen to “My Cathedral” and “Something Strange” in my car on the way to work, so I was psyched when Ben was booked to play with all of us in Jersey City. I think we hit it off immediately; I could tell Ben just got it, it being the reason we all do what we do as artists. It’s really cool when you meet someone and are on the same wavelength. Stare Away. Photo by Constant Williams Constant and Ben, did you initially connect through any shared bands, records, or influences, and what helped that first connection develop? Ben: Definitely comparing our distinguished sounds to similar bands we both enjoy, I think Joy Division would be a top example because we both love Ian Curtis’ writing from a poetic standpoint, we did hit the exhibit in New York City together which was an awesome experience. I always learn of new books and readings to pick up from him. I also think it’s because I am a bassist and he came from a background of being a drummer, so I think a lot of bands that have that heavy foundation of rhythm sections drove a lot of our similar musical interests. Constant: For sure, I think most people who make music similar to us can connect over a shared love of many of the same bands (like the ones I mentioned before). I think it also helped that we both come to music at a poetic and existential angle, and we both could relate in terms of recovery from substances and the perspective shift that is required. Constant and Ben, what first made you want to collaborate musically, and when did the idea of touring together enter the conversation? We haven’t collaborated yet but we definitely have a song in the works. I think every time we’ve seen each other, we’ve thrown around the idea of touring together because we love each other’s music, and it especially made sense now that both of us are with BLCKJEANS. Ben, what appeals to you most about Reducer, and which song from the record do you find yourself returning to most often? I think Constants approach on the arrangements were genius. The drum breaks feel lyrical, the combination of synth selections and vocal melodies reached a part of this genre that hasn’t been touched upon yet, and classic Casket Cassette elements cultivated into his best work. My favorite part of all this is watching and listening as an artist grows musically. It’s hard to put my finger on a single song because each song has its own unique skeleton, but I have to go with “Apathy” as the track that’s always running through my head on this record. Constant, what do you enjoy most about In Absence, and which song on the album has become your personal favorite? Beyond how catchy and danceable its songs are, I love how authentic and genuine the album is. I also really enjoy the combination of quintessential 80’s New Wave sounds with dark Post-Punk melodies. The title track and Faithless Hum are my top favorites. Constant and Ben, your music shares certain post-punk and darkwave foundations while retaining two distinct identities. What do you think makes the bands complement each other so well on the same bill? Ben: I think our high-energy performances are what make this tour so special; the riffs throughout the night keep the atmosphere intense with movement and bring a great amount of nostalgia you feel at a goth club or punk show that you can’t capture at other shows. Our deep connection with the fans is what’s most important to me, hearing how the music can move through the audience and watching kids get lost in their dancing with their eyes closed while we’re playing on stage is so cool being able to resonate that from the stage. Constant: I think we complement each other because we both bring a similar energetic performance style, matching high energy with a candid sincerity. Ben’s music leans more towards post-punk with moments of darkwave, while my music leans more towards darkwave with moments of post-punk. I think that also creates a “yin and yang” effect for our live shows; two sides of the same coin. Casket Cassette. Photo by Aaron Jay Young Constant, you come from Los Angeles, while Ben is based in New York City. How have the music scenes and cultures of those cities shaped your respective projects, and what similarities do you recognize between them? And what do you think is different? Ben: I think New York City’s music scene is so diverse, which makes it such a beautiful and thriving location for musicians and showgoers. You can hit a punk show, an electronic show, hardcore show, or jazz club in the same borough in the same night. It’s wicked, I love it. I think LA is quite the same besides the traffic haha, but I think the diversity of people and genres is the best and most important similarity of both cities, keeping live music thriving. New York City in general has a million places to find and take inspiration from. Taking late night subway rides can create a huge narrative story in its own way, walking in the parks and seeing all different types of fashion and taking everyone’s unique sense of expression and sensing love and unfortunate disparities throughout the air can present all kinds of thoughts and ideas to put down on paper, it becomes its own dimension and reality that spews inspiration for lyrics and especially beat and rhythm. The nightlife through dive bars and street festivities is an overwhelming resource of artistic relation. You can simply sit in a moment, look around, and take in so much that you can’t find anywhere else. I try to take the mood and energy of wherever I was that night or night before to the writing process to resemble the city’s grit and hardstyle energy that keeps it alive. Constant: I think growing up in Los Angeles has informed my music a lot. There’s a strange duality to the shiny movie stars, warm beaches, and perpetual sunshine that is surrounded by industrial decay, violence, and broken dreams. I think my music has a similar duality, being both deeply sad and deeply danceable. That’s a strange combo that (I hope) works. It definitely reflects how I grew up and who I am; I never truly fit into any one box. On the contrary, despite being visually more gothic and less “shiny” than LA, I feel as though the scene might be a bit less substantial in size in New York City, but I only know a little from my limited experience. It has always made me laugh that the places with the most goths are often the ones that punish us with bright sunlight (ie. Los Angeles, Mexico City, San Antonio, etc., with the exception of Chicago). I love New York, and I do think there is a kinship between the two cities, and certainly they are two of the most important musical hubs in the world. Constant and Ben, what are you each most excited about on this run, and what kind of experience do you hope audiences take away from seeing both projects in the same room? Ben: I’m really stoked to finally play these new songs live and also give the fans a chance to sing the songs that got us here with us. My absolute favorite part is inspiring younger showgoers to keep pushing their craft; the young musicians are the main reason I do this 100%. I started going to shows around 12-13 years old at VFWs and want to relive how I felt when people rushed to the stage to snag the mic from the vocalist to scream the lyrics. We want to go against the grain as much as possible so we get sweaty with everyone on stage with us during ‘Parting Ways’. It just started out of a last-minute call-up on our first show in San Diego so I just wanted to try and accomplish that every single night regardless of the size of the audience. I was pretty nervous at first, but I know the fans have such a fun time being able to dance underneath the lights with us, and that’s what matters the most. I hope the audience can take away a fresh new ear for Post-Punk music and can feel like they’re at a Factory or CBGB show. I just want people to feel free in a safe space and take home an amazing show experience. Constant: I’m excited to play shows with Stare Away and all our awesome local openers because I know the audience is going to have a great experience! As my first headliner tour, I’m also really excited to get to play a longer set for fans; I’m always bummed when someone comes up to say hi and is sad that I didn’t play a specific song; hopefully having a fuller set mitigates some of that disappointment. Another favorite part of tour for me is meeting the amazing people who listen to my music; none of this would be possible without them, and they mean everything to me. All I want is for them to have a night where they can let go and enjoy themselves during these crazy times. Constant and Ben, once the tour is over and both albums have had time to settle into the world, what does each of you have planned for 2027, and do you envision further collaborations? Ben: As soon as we get back, I plan on just getting right back to constructing the direction of the next record. I want to find the perfect hybrid kit to add to our live shows and just make something different. I feel like a lot of bands just get trapped in the same sound, playing the same riffs. I definitely want to get my head into a new book and maybe pick up some weird new hobby, but I think I just want to challenge myself towards a new direction to take Stare Away. Constant: I recently won a literary award, and as a result I will be releasing a book of poetry in 2027 called Elegy with Beautiful Child, available for preorder from Milkweed Editions. My lifelong dream (even before music) has always been to publish a book of poetry, so this is a really important moment in my life! There is also a Stare Away x Casket Cassette song in the works, and Ben and I are good friends, so it’s definitely not the last you’ll be hearing from both of us.§ Casket Cassette’s Reducer is out now. Listen below, and Order Here. REDUCER by Casket Cassette Stare Away’s In Absence is out now. Listen below and Order Here. In Absence by Stare Away The end of the Reducer tour leaves both artists with fresh work already taking shape. Nelson plans to begin developing the next Stare Away record as soon as he returns to New York, introducing a hybrid drum kit while pushing the project toward unfamiliar methods. Williams will turn toward the January 2027 publication of Elegy with Beautiful Child, his debut poetry collection and winner of the 2025–26 Jake Adam York Prize. A Stare Away and Casket Cassette song is also underway, extending a friendship that began on a shared bill into the studio. Before those plans take over, Casket Cassette and Stare Away have eight dates remaining together on Casket Cassette’s Reducer Tour. The itinerary continues August 12 at Beat Kitchen in Chicago, followed by Minneapolis, Denver, Salt Lake City, Seattle, Portland, and San Francisco before their shared run closes August 22 at Summer Fox Brewing – Tower in Fresno. items.body:
Peak Oil sublabel FO returns with a strong debut of late night, air-fried trip hop from Cold Light, flocking like moths to an illbient flame tipped FFO Jabu, Tricky, Sleepdial, Shell Company, Space Afrika.

Cold Light are Bristol’s Birthmark & Withdrawn, Portland’s Best Available Technology, Rael & Eldon out of London, and Hungarian CSNL. Some half a decade after a ‘Live at the Laundromat’ tape introduction, the collective unveil ‘Coldtron 2’, a sparingly sensuous slant on the lush pastures between trip hop, smoked-out dub soul and illbient jazz, inflected with the voices of Elaine Malone, Akeko and British-Nigerian sound designer Tony Onuchukwu. With remarkable restraint - especially considering so many hands are on board - they keep everything pared-back to creaking, atmospheric fundamentals for 40 minutes of smouldering storytelling, passing the torch across chapters of zoot-end poetic monologues, from stylised rap to spoken word, in a spectrum of accents speaking to the group’s far flung coordinates. 

Call it downbeat neo-noir or trip hop 2.0, the sound is clearly in thrall to the ‘90s OGs - Tricky, Portishead, Massive Attack - yet gauzily distinguished from its forebears by the production’s pall of dematerialised textures and an enervated feel for screwed subs and glimmers of sounds that emerged in trip hop’s fall-out. The Bristol night air is thick with sferic crackle and diffused sax in ’Smoke Signal’ thru the Memotone-esque eldritch of ‘Troposphere Test’, taking in a tacit nod to Mobb Deep via Tricky on the smouldering ‘Riot’, or even Civilistjävel!’s low-key electrodub in ‘Lean Wid It…’,    and Sleepdial’s slurred drums on ‘I’ve Known Fires’. But they’re most potent on ‘Fields in B’ with eight mins of smudged Rhythm & Sound steppas bass anchoring the bluest sax plumes and blunted bars, ideal for ashtray dreamers.

items._cn_summary: 这是Peak Oil子厂牌FO推出的跨国集体作品Cold Light的首张正式专辑，由来自布里斯托尔、波特兰、伦敦和匈牙利的五位音乐人合作完成，跨越五年打磨。专辑在trip hop、烟熏dub灵魂乐与illbient爵士之间开辟出稀疏而感性的地带，邀请多位客座人声贡献者参与，从风格化说唱到口语诗歌，以多元口音呼应成员的国际背景。制作上虽汇聚众多合作者，却保持克制，四十分钟内仅以氛围化的基础元素铺陈，sferic噪音、弥漫的萨克斯、模糊的低频和粘稠的鼓点交错出现。明显受90年代trip hop前辈影响，却以去物质化的质感纹理区别开来，诸如'Fields in B'中八分钟的闷烧节奏与蓝调萨克斯片段，以及对Civilistjävel!式electrodub的致敬，均展现其独特的暗夜美学。

items.body:
Songs Before Bed (2022),  Otto Benson’s first physical release under his own name, following earlier work under aliases including Memo Boy, OTTO, and Pudding Club.

"Originally published as a digital-only release through Otto's own WNOADIARWB website and platforms on New Year's Eve 2022, Songs Before Bed bridges the gap between the more experimental psychedelic electronic works of OTTO and his most recent release, the acclaimed Peanut, released on NYE 2025. Blending brief pop fragments with melodic bedroom guitar, droning ambient shoegaze textures, and blissful IDM jaunts reminiscent of the Rephlex catalog, the album offers a seamless overview of Otto Benson's genre-defying sound. Originally conceived as a late-night record, Songs Before Bed (2022) rewards listening at any hour."
items._genre: experimental electronic / ambient shoegaze / IDM / bedroom pop
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Otto Benson以本名发行的首张实体作品，此前他曾以多个化名活动。专辑融合了简短的流行片段与卧室吉他旋律，并交织着持续音环境质地与鞋垫失真音墙，呈现出IDM风格的跳跃感，明显带有Rephlex厂牌系的美学痕迹。作为一张原本构思为深夜聆听的作品，它跨越了从实验迷幻电子到卧室流行的多种风格，展现了作者跨越类型边界的声音全貌。整张专辑在编制上保持紧凑，既有旋律性的亲切感，也保留了抽象的声响探索，适合在安静时段反复聆听。

items.body:
All killer, no filler trotters from a golden period of Lee ‘Scratch’ Perry’s foundational work at fabled studio, The Black Ark.

This 3rd in a prized series spies the wee madman conjuring multidimensional spectres from vocal recordings of regular spars: Max Romeo, The Jolly Brothers, Leroy Sibbles, The Mistic, and Devon Irons. Perry’s visionary, innovative application of studio-as-instrument tekkerz come to the fore in the music’s layered diffusions, which we may take for granted in contemporary music, but was radical back then, and whose uncanny appeal has only steeped with age. 

Including a solo standout in the ghostly, harmonised roots wooze of his ‘Dread Lion’ gem as King Scratch, it spans the signature, lysergic sparkle of his ‘Conscious Man’cut with The Jolly Brothers, thru a stepping 12” mix of Max Romeo’s ‘Norman’ (1978), and heat-hazed sway to Leroy Sibbles’ ‘Garden of Life’, along with The Mistic’s eyes-down devotional ‘Forward With Jah’, and sloshing nyabingi of ‘When Jah Comes’ for Devon Irons.
items._cn_summary: 本合辑收录了李·佩里在黑方舟录音室1977至1979年间制作的五首经典迪斯科混音作品，将Max Romeo、The Jolly Brothers、Leroy Sibbles等歌手的人声素材通过多轨分层、混响与延迟处理，转化为充满迷幻色彩与空间纵深的声场。佩里将录音棚本身视为乐器的实验性手法在当代虽已被广泛沿用，但在当时具有开创性意义。曲目涵盖深沉灵性的和声罗茨、跳跃的十二寸混音版以及朦胧摇摆的雷鬼律动，整体呈现出浓烈的迷幻氛围与宗教式冥想质感。作为黑方舟系列的第三卷，该合辑以考古式策展方式重现了这座传奇录音棚最具创造力的时期。

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是赞比亚出生、南非成长的艺术家ムーンガ・K.的首张作品，核心概念颇为独特：以2153年为起点向70年代回溯，演奏带有非洲未来主义色彩的放克与灵魂乐。乐评指出其影响来源清晰可辨——Funkadelic的迷幻放克、Stevie Wonder的灵魂传统、Prince的流行敏感度均有所体现。在这两条线索之外，专辑还穿插了爽快的迪斯科段落和柔和的雷鬼作品，展现出作者在风格跨度上的灵活性。整体而言，这是一张概念驱动、跨风格取材的非洲未来主义流行音乐作品。

items._cn_summary: 缪斯乐队第十张专辑与曾为Bring Me the Horizon等乐队担纲制作的Dan Lancaster合作，在金属与前卫摇滚的演奏基底上叠加赛博风格元素。专辑呈现出宏大的声场构建与类型融合策略——《Nightshift Superstar》走交响电子路线，《Hush》与Ellie Goulding合作则偏向哥特EDM曲风，听感上追求吞噬式的包裹体验。全英八连冠的纪录显示这是一张主流定位明确的作品，制作精良但更偏向商业化大型摇滚的延伸，而非先锋实验。该评论原文偏短，信息量有限，难以对专辑的创新程度做更深入判断。整体而言，对暗潮与电子融合爱好者有一定参考价值，但距离真正的前卫实验语境仍有距离。

This might be the best of them. The music is so many-sided and eclectic that each listen brings something new. Some of my favourites ... though this is an album that needs to be played from start to finish: Morning at Boma Park - upbeat and Afro-jazzyThe title track - great atmosphereIn Doga Gamee - starts out with classical piano and gradually builds with some beautiful motifsPassage to Promise - gentle African music that's a great contrast to the pervious trackJuggler in Obsidian - super tasty flamencoChanson de L'Heure Bleue leading into Czippa and the Ursania Girl - just beautifulThe album isn't so much a "Masterpiece of prog rock" so much as an eclectic masterpiece of world music with prog elements, so four stars.
items._genre: world fusion / crossover prog / new age

items.body: Perverts in White Shirts, the Zurich-based experimental electronic duo of Nathalie Dreier and Dave Phillips, will release the 2CD “CULTurally appropriated songs and revisited memories” on September 4, 2026 through Misanthropic Agenda. The 28-track, roughly two-hour album reworks source material connected to Dreier’s upbringing in the Children of God cult, alongside songs and texts drawn from other fringe religious movements and groups built around charismatic leaders. Perverts in White Shirts rework cult songs on ‘CULTurally appropriated songs and revisited memories’ Dreier and Phillips rework, decontextualize and reimagine melodies and words originally tied to ideology, isolation and indoctrination, blurring the lines between belief and manipulation, intimacy and control, devotion and performance. Misanthropic Agenda describes the record as “a two-hour cringe-pop journey.” The tracklist includes “What A Wonderful World We Live In,” “Love Is The Only Weapon,” “Truth,” “Come To Mommy” and “The Fear Of God,” and closes with “Shangri-La,” a 28-minute, 59-second track. The album was recorded in Zurich between 2024 and 2025 and mastered by Riccardo Mazza. Misanthropic Agenda is also issuing Vincent Grimaldi’s “Amorce De Champ” on the same September 4, 2026 release date. CULTurally appropriated songs and revisited memories by Perverts In White Shirts About Perverts in White Shirts Perverts in White Shirts is the collaborative project of Nathalie Dreier and Dave Phillips, active since 2011 and based in Zurich. Phillips is a Swiss experimental noise musician and multimedia artist who performs as a core member of Schimpfluch-Gruppe, the Zurich collective founded in 1987, and who also founded the grindcore group Fear of God and the project OHNE. Perverts in White Shirts released their debut album, “Power to the Sheeple,” in 2016, followed by “Meaning What Exactly?” in June 2022, an album recorded in Zurich and Berlin between 2016 and 2020 and issued in a limited edition of 100 copies through Misanthropic Agenda. The duo combine treated field recordings with acoustic and digital sources, with music described across outlets as electro, industrial, witch house, experimental and noise pop. “CULTurally appropriated songs and revisited memories,” due September 4, 2026, is the duo’s third full-length and their first to draw directly on Dreier’s own upbringing within the Children of God cult.
items._genre: experimental electronic / industrial / noise pop / witch house

items.body: Dariusz Jackowski, a composer and multi-instrumentalist based in Wroclaw, Poland, released the EP “Bezimienny” through the Wroclaw label Ubocze Rec. The four-track release takes its title from the Polish word for “nameless,” and each track carries a different-language equivalent of that word, in Polish, Japanese, Turkmen and Zulu. All instruments and ideas on the EP are credited to Jackowski himself. Stylistically, “Bezimienny” moves between film and theatre music, building a suggestive, tension-filled soundscape. Almost orchestral passages, built from choral voices and bells, are set against the heavy sound of distorted, droning guitar, giving the four compositions a strong sense of drama. The Japanese-titled track “Nanashi,” meaning “nameless,” carries an unsettling, western-tinged atmosphere that draws on the spirit of Ennio Morricone’s film work, filtered through Jackowski’s own musical language. Bezimienny by Dariusz Jackowski Dariusz Jackowski explores anonymity on ‘Bezimienny’ The theme of anonymity runs through the EP’s four track titles, each a different language’s word for “nameless.” Ubocze Rec. describes the release as moving between soundtrack and haunt-leaning electronic music, pairing orchestral elements with distorted guitar textures. About Dariusz Jackowski Dariusz Jackowski is a composer, improviser and multi-instrumentalist based in Wroclaw, Poland, who also works as a sound and music computing researcher, music software developer, and mixing and mastering engineer. He performs as part of the group Monument Zero and has released a series of solo works through Ubocze Rec., including “Not for People,” “Colours of Wind,” “Mikrodawkowanie” (with DustCats) and “Bleach Cocktail.” “Bezimienny” continues that run of releases on the label, built entirely from Jackowski’s own instrumentation and production.
items._cn_summary: 波兰作曲家兼多乐器演奏家Dariusz Jackowski发行四曲EP，标题取自波兰语"无名"，四首曲目分别以波兰语、日语、土库曼语和祖鲁语命名同一概念，主题贯穿"匿名性"。所有乐器与构想均由Jackowski独自完成。音乐风格游走于电影与剧场配乐之间，构建充满暗示性与张力的音景。近似管弦乐的段落以合唱声部与钟声构建，却与失真嗡鸣的吉他声形成对峙，营造出强烈的戏剧感。其中日语标题的"Nanashi"呈现出受Morricone西部片配乐影响的诡异氛围，并融入个人化语汇。整体结合管弦乐元素与失真吉他质感，倾向于配乐与暗潮电子之间的混合表达。

items.body: Cliff and Ivy, the goth duo from Anchorage, Alaska, released their ten-track album “Angels Eyes” on August 7, 2026, on the band’s own label, House of Extreme Darkness. The record revisits classic goth rock while adding deathrock, post-punk and metal elements. Angels Eyes by Cliff and Ivy “Angels Eyes” runs “Lockdown”, “The Healer”, “The Raven and The Wolf”, “Tidalwaves”, “Of Love and The Rain”, “Kiss of Death”, “Black Pyramid”, “The Collapse”, “Stone and Mind” and “Propaganda”, with a digital/CD bonus track, “The Healer Alt Mix”. The album is available on streaming platforms, CD and vinyl, with physical media, merchandise and downloads sold through the band’s Bandcamp page. Cliff Livingston wrote and arranged the songs and plays guitars and bass, while Ivy Silence handles lyrics, vocals, art and design. The sessions brought in guest drummer Tom Coyne, who also plays in 45 Grave and Kommunity FK, and multi-instrumentalist Paul Roessler, known for his work with the Nina Hagen Band and The Screamers, who produced, engineered, mixed and played keyboards, piano and synth on the record at Kitten Robot Studio in Los Angeles. Maor Appelbaum, a Grammy-nominated engineer, mastered the album. ‘The Raven and The Wolf’ and the album’s themes “The Raven and The Wolf” pairs piano, rock drums and guitar riffs around the image of a raven and a wolf as archetypal lovers. “We wanted to capture the feeling of love that’s wild, eternal, and a little dangerous,” Ivy Silence said of the song. “It’s about finding someone who sees your shadow and still chooses to stay.” “The Healer” honors a nurse who spent decades caring for children and families in remote parts of Alaska, built around piano and guitar swells. “Lockdown” addresses isolation and confinement through distorted guitars and pounding rhythms, while “Propaganda” carries a political edge and “Kiss of Death” leans into deathrock with the line “Everything born begins to decay.” About Cliff and Ivy Cliff Livingston and Ivy Silence, originally from New Jersey, have made music together since the 1980s, working through hardcore, post-punk and experimental projects before settling in Anchorage in 1993. They formed Cliff and Ivy in 2011 and built their catalogue independently from Alaska, drawing on ritual imagery and the state’s wilderness for their sound and visuals. The duo released the EP “Bring Us The Night” in 2021, followed by the single “Die Tonight” in 2023 and “We Ignite“, a collaboration with a guitarist from The Smithereens, later that year. In 2024 they issued “Sinister Stars” on vinyl with several collaborators, and in October 2025 they previewed the new record with the two-track EP “Angels Eyes: Singles“. “Angels Eyes”, released August 7, 2026, is their first full album since “Sinister Stars” and continues the collaborative approach of past releases, with credits from Tom Coyne and Paul Roessler among others.
items._cn_summary: 来自阿拉斯加安克雷奇的二人组合Cliff and Ivy发布了十曲专辑《Angels Eyes》，以经典哥特摇滚为基底，融入死亡摇滚、后朋克与金属元素。专辑由吉他贝斯手Cliff Livingston撰写编曲，主唱Ivy Silence负责词作演唱及视觉设计，特邀鼓手Tom Coyne与曾参与Nina Hagen Band的Paul Roessler担任制作并演奏键盘钢琴。母带由格莱美提名工程师Maor Appelbaum处理。《The Raven and The Wolf》以钢琴摇滚架构隐喻野性之爱，《The Healer》致敬阿拉斯加偏远地区护士，《Lockdown》用失真吉他表现隔离主题，《Kiss of Death》则强调万物衰败的死亡摇滚美学。专辑在自有厂牌House of Extreme Darkness发行，物理介质通过Bandcamp销售，整体保持了地下独立姿态但在风格融合上偏传统哥特框架内运作。

items.body: Redemption the salvation That’s out of reach All the lies they will forever preach The night belongs to vampires, black leather, bad blood, and decisions best made after the sun has gone down. The Lost Boys sank its fangs into theatres on the 31 of July 1987, and Karlsruhe industrial death wave trio Bleak Monday chose the same date 39 years later to unleash Shelter. It feels like an appropriately cursed bit of calendar alignment. The song and its accompanying video share the film’s appetite for danger, nocturnal excess, temptation, and the enduring truth that everyone looks better once respectable society has locked its doors and drawn the curtains. Bleak Monday takes that invitation underground, descending into a dungeon club where the congregation wears black, the entertainment comes with cages, and somebody has clearly misplaced both the fire code and the holy water. Bleak Monday formed in Karlsruhe in December 2022 with one foot in ’80s wave and the other planted somewhere between metal, industrial rock, and the more bruising end of electronic music. Skinny Puppy, Nine Inch Nails, and Ministry provide useful coordinates, though there is also enough dangerous glamour here to imagine the song turning up midway through a particularly depraved Gregg Araki sequence. Directed by Natascha Gaballo, the video drops Bleak Monday into a dungeon club populated by cages, goth go-go dancers, temptation, domination, and enough black vinyl to make a parish priest reconsider his evening plans. The footage was transferred to VHS and then re-digitized, giving the images the bruised texture of an ’80s B-movie that spent several years behind the counter at a video store before somebody finally asked what was on it. Horror references tied to singer Kim Ryder’s favorite films are tucked into the scenery for anyone inclined to freeze-frame their way through the debauchery. That presentation suits Shelter, a slab of industrial death wave built from Yann Lauer’s guitar, Sebastian “Hubu” Huber’s synths, drums, and bass, and Ryder’s commanding vocal performance. Ryder sings about religious hypocrisy, concealed abuse, televised violence, and salvation sold by institutions that appear to have misplaced the receipt. The central plea for rescue grows increasingly desperate as the song works through shame, faith, exploitation, and spiritual exhaustion. Any promise of redemption feels compromised by the people making it, leaving the singer caught between belief, disgust, and the desire to disappear from a reality that has become unbearable. Gaballo makes that unease physical. Ryder performs amid bodies presented as spectacle, pleasure, threat, and distraction, while the club becomes both sanctuary and trap. The cages are hardly subtle, but subtlety would be rather pointless when the song is throwing death, rape, hypocrisy, and redemption into the room. Sometimes a sledgehammer has admirable editorial instincts. Watch the video for Shelter below: Shelter also serves as a teaser for Bleak Monday’s forthcoming debut album, Bad Music, a title that practically invites hostile witnesses. Since beginning live shows in early 2023, the trio have shared stages with Das Kinn, Nils Keppel, The Body, and Ministry. Judging from this clip, they have already figured out one valuable lesson: if civilization is collapsing, somebody should at least book the dancers. Listen to Shelter below and order the single here. Shelter by Bleak Monday Follow Bleak Monday: Instagram Facebook Bandcamp YouTube Spotify The post “Burn the Lies” — Karlsruhe Industrial Death Wave Trio Bleak Monday Unleashes Video for Shelter” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
items._cn_summary: Bleak Monday 是一支来自德国卡尔斯鲁厄的三人乐队，成立于2022年末，音乐融合八十年代暗潮、工业摇滚与电子乐的粗粝质感，参照对象包括 Skinny Puppy、Nine Inch Nails 与 Ministry。《Shelter》以吉他的金属重量、合成器的冷峻层次与极具压迫感的人声交织而成，歌词聚焦宗教伪善、隐蔽的暴力、媒介化的残酷与被出售的救赎，核心诉求在羞耻、信仰与精神倦怠之间逐渐瓦解。MV 由 Natascha Gaballo 执导，地牢俱乐部场景中出现铁笼、哥特舞者与黑色乙烯基材质，影像经 VHS 转录再数字化处理，呈现八十年代B级片般的磨损颗粒感。制作并未走向极端实验，而是在类型框架内以强烈的视觉叙事与主题重量强化听觉冲击，对暗潮与工业受众有明确的类型吸引力。

items._cn_summary: Roy Montgomery与Martha Skye Murphy合作专辑《Nebular》延续了二人各自的音乐脉络，创作出一组宽银幕式的梦境流行长篇作品。二人因一盒混音带结缘，发现彼此在创作方法上的共通点——都使用Tascam多轨录音机——由此发展出和谐的创作关系。专辑融合了二人各自的优势，形成一种充满张力的艺术熔炉，参考对象包括Cocteau Twins、Harold Budd的梦幻气质，Flying Saucer Attack的朦胧声响，Jessamine的缓慢展开以及lovesliescrushing的细腻纹理。整体呈现出宽广音景与碎片化声响交织的特点，介于独立梦泡与氛围即兴之间，但专辑偏向dream pop类型传统，与用户关注的实验、前卫、暗潮等口味存在一定距离。

items.body: Epstein As a writer, researcher, musician, composer, and artist in the public sphere, Melvin Gibbs seems to have been working towards something like How Black Music Took Over the World for while now—a synthesizing work that brings together personal history, polemic, Black music made in and beyond America both under and in spite of a racialized cultural hierarchy, and the heartbreak and joy that come with learning and acknowledging this shared (like it or not) history. How that synthesis enacts itself on paper is one of Gibbs’s particular skills, his melding of register (as he lays out in the Prelude) replays his musical practice. An open reader who lets the book take over will be, I think inarguably, rewarded. One of the key areas that’s under-discussed in literature, as far as I’m aware, which Gibbs both personally and academically goes over in the book is the Gullah-Geechee, the community rooted in the Sea Islands, along the Georgia and Florida coast. In the chapters “Stono’s Children” and “Changing Time With the Times,” Gibbs recounts his discovery of his Gullah heritage, then takes readers on a fascinating journey of the elemental components of rhythm, from ring shout, hambone, swing, and backbeat, to dub. What works pretty well in idea—merging registers, mixing personal memoir with rhythmic analysis—plays out (pardon the unintentional pun) wonderfully on paper. From an extended rhythmic analysis in “Stono’s Children,” Gibbs drops us right into a Harriet Tubman rehearsal. In a later chapter “Can’t Stop,” Gibbs breaks down a specific rhythm he’s dubbed the “lunch table cell,” then demonstrates its use in school lunch ad libs, James Brown’s “Soul Power,” Fela Kuti’s “Shakara,” and Led Zeppelin’s “When the Levee Breaks.” There’s a joy in taking all this in, and the infectious enthusiasm Gibbs seems to take in sharing the rhythms and ideas he’s studied and generated. “The Music of Black Science” demonstrates the linkage from mythos developed through sharing stories to cosmologies that underpin systems of belief, math, science, and artistry. As a somewhat mystical rumination on West African frameworks, and what Gibbs describes as an ontology of Black music. The ensuing pages explore mythologies, fables, and physics through the lens of oral communication and visualization. It’s one of the chapters I’ve dipped back into multiple times, letting myself drift to and fro, which doesn’t seem to contradict Gibb’s intent. However intentional, or not, How Black Music Took Over the World is in conversation with two crucial writers and researchers in this area, Race Music by Guthrie Ramsey and Blacksound by Matthew Morrison. Ramsey’s been in the space for over 30 years building up a compelling and provocative (for me, personally, I’m using this word in terms of “provoking intellectual thought and reflection”) body of work, and Morrison’s Blacksound is the kind of seminal work that hopefully becomes required reading for anyone seeking to understand the acoustical aspects of blackface minstrelsy that became the bedrock of the recording industry. Much like Gibbs’s assembly of evidence showing Black performance and foundational rhythms permeating styles and genres, Morrison demonstrates how Blacksound (re-)centers the ephemeral sonic and performance aesthetics that were capitalized on by early white adopters of vaudeville and dance. While no single author can be expected to cover all aspects of a topic, there are areas Gibbs elides or leaves out of his narrative that are readily picked up in these two—and, yes, many other—books, which an earnest reader is encouraged to also seek out. items._cn_summary: Melvin Gibbs的著作《How Black Music Took Over the World》将个人回忆录与节奏分析相结合，追溯黑人音乐的全球影响。书中探讨了Gullah-Geechee社区的根源，从ring shout、hambone、swing到backbeat和dub等节奏元素的演变。Gibbs通过具体案例分析，如将「lunch table cell」节奏在James Brown、Fela Kuti和Led Zeppelin作品中的运用，展现了跨文化的节奏传承。「The Music of the Black Science」章节从西非神话和口述传统出发，探讨黑人音乐本体论中神话、数学与艺术的关联。整体而言，这是一部融合学术研究、个人叙事与文化批评的作品，与Guthrie Ramsey的《Race Music》和Matthew Morrison的《Blacksound》形成对话，为理解黑人音乐的历史脉络与全球扩散提供了独特视角。

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. More to hear: United States of Alchemy - Songs of Compassion (Review) Dani Jan� - Vida (Review)

items.body:
A debut, digital-only EP from a Danish trio, led by one of the Nordic folk scene�s outstanding and experienced vocalists, Mia Guldhammer. Five tracks, with the musicians bringing their own perspectives to mostly traditional music. There�s a lovely ancient, creaky mood throughout.
The opener, �Svennedal,� with its rough, cantering rhythm, offers a perfect shop window for Guldhammer�s impressive, persuasive voice, while jaw harp and bagpipes bring an insistent propulsion to �Nordg�rd,� the only original here, by band member Morten Musicus.
Cimbalom adds a delicate backdrop to the traditional �Agnete Of Bjergmanden,� with Guldhammer�s soft jaw harp offering extra textures to the other instruments, as it brings a springy opening to the final cut, �Orms�,� mingling with flute and strings to create something quite thrilling and off kilter on this instrumental.
Five tracks, and an introduction to a band that already seems very mature and accomplished. A strong beginning � what will GuldGanger do with an entire album?
items.label: Go' Danish Folk Music
items._cn_summary: 这张数字EP是丹麦三人组合GuldGanger的首发作品，由北欧民谣圈资深主唱Mia Guldhammer领衔。五首曲目大多取材自传统音乐，乐手各自带入不同诠释。开篇曲《Svennedal》节奏粗犷奔腾，充分展示了Guldhammer极具说服力的嗓音；《Nordgård》是唯一的原创作品，加入口琴与风笛形成强劲推进力。传统曲目《Agnete Of Bjergmanden》以扬琴铺设精致背景，收尾曲《Ormsö》则是纯器乐演奏，口琴与长笛、弦乐交织，呈现出令人兴奋的失衡感。整体弥漫着古老、吱嘎作响的氛围，五首作品已展现出乐队的成熟度与完成度。虽以传统民谣为底，但器乐编配与非常规乐器组合赋予作品一定的实验色彩。

items.body: Editor's note: When this set of recordings came to me, I was at a loss as to how to share it. It's not music, in any traditional sense (although there is some freestyle rapping), and a 'review' of such an artifact of reality seems superfluous to the content. Instead, I asked sound recordist Ian Brennan if I could simply use his own brief commentary and the recordings he made on the street in Chicago. Twenty-five people afflicted by gun violence participated, many from the very block we�d setup on. Many neighbors were pulled-in spontaneously. Almost every one in the community had been impacted by violence somehow� both on the receiving and the inflicting end, and many both. One woman had just come from a memorial service, another was on her way. That�s how far-reaching the violence. Almost no one went untouched. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors By chance, we convened on the day that Trump ordered the deployment of the National Guard to the city. The recording took place on the front porch of the leader's ninety-four-year-old grandmother's house�right in the heart of the ��hood,� beneath the Midway Airport�s landing path. A pair of stray pitfalls stalked the block. But the grandmother warned not of gunshots, but the mosquitoes in her yard. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors We were in a section of town that one man defined as �the forgotten parts.� Just a short jaunt from the designer clothes shops and posh hotels of the city�s Magnificent Mile, the Southside spawned such legendary Blues artists as Muddy Waters, Willie Dixon, and Howlin� Wolf. Jazz musicians like Lionel Hampton and even Benny Goodman, hailed from nearby. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors The participants ranged in age from seventeen to sixty-seven, but the pattern held true. The person who�d asserted �you�ll really want to hear my story,� was the least compelling. The reluctant, the most moving. One elder�s tough facade broke down as she shared how she�d lost both her sons. She tearfully apologized, �I�m sorry. I�m sorry. I�m sorry.� But she had nothing to be sorry for. Society is the one that owes the apology� for the staggering statistical inequities of which no reasonable defense can be made. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors Editor's note: The full set of recordings are available on Bandcamp. Any profits from this project will be donated to Cure Violence Global , who states that their mission is "advancing an evidence-based health approach to end violence globally." When I asked him about the background sounds, producer Ian Brennan added, "No music is added. It�s all sounds from the source environment. I also ran loops/drones on a different track in the background as they spoke, and when they ended up being incidentally/somewhat magically/eerily synchronous, that is what was used for a few pieces with 'accompaniment' like some of the rap freestyles."
items._genre: field recording / spoken word / sound documentary
items._cn_summary: 这不是传统意义上的音乐专辑，而是录音师Ian Brennan在芝加哥南区街头录制的声音文献。25位枪支暴力幸存者参与了录制，地点选在94岁祖母家门前廊下，正值特朗普下令派遣国民警卫队入城的同一天。录音中没有任何添加的音乐，所有声音均来自现场环境，参与者年龄从17岁到67岁不等。内容主要是对话与独白讲述，包括一位老人因失去两个儿子而崩溃道歉的场景。专辑透过最直接的田野录音揭示芝加哥南区——孕育了Muddy Waters等布鲁斯传奇艺术家之地——所承受的暴力创伤。所有收益将捐赠给Cure Violence Global组织。

items.body: Review by yarstruly — This review is simultaneously published on my blog (Scott's Song by Song Spotlights with links and additional information).Enigmatic Sound Machines (ESM) are a collaboration between Jeremie Arrobas (a founding member of Men Without Hats) and Thomas Szirmay (a prog musicologist, researcher, producer, arranger, actor, vocalist and writer). They are based in Montreal, Quebec, Canada. This is their fourth album since their 2023 debut. According to the information I have received, ESM: "is a retro-futuristic project, the brainchild of two childhood friends with a common love for music, philosophy, and the arts." Today I'll be reviewing their 4th album "Divided by One".Over the years, they have expanded to become a 4-piece band. The line-up for this album is as follows.- Jeremie Arrobas/ lead vocals, synth guitars, keyboards, sound machines- Thomas Szirmay /enigmatic voice and sound machines- Alain Bellaiche/ guitars . backing vocals- Hansford Rowe / bass and backing vocalsGuest artists :- Steve Bonino/guitars (1,6)- Roland Buhlmann/ guitars (7)- Anna Arrobas / backing vocals (1,3,4,7)- Laura Piazzai/ lead vocals (8)- Quinn Bachand / violin (8) This album was provided by Anne-Claire Rallo of Bad Dog Promotions. As always, I receive no further compensation, and I call it like I hear it. As per my usual method, this is a cold listen.Let's listen and find out what all of that means!!Track 1 - Divided by One (6:16)After a few sound effects, a steady drumbeat begins, soon joined by some cool fretless bass work. They lock into a groove, and the guitar plays power chords (Steve Bonino?). Jeramie joins with lead vocals soon after. There is a slight Pink Floyd feel in some ways. The tempo is moderate and the bass part gives it a slightly funky feel. I believe Thomas' "Enigmatic Voice" is in the choruses. I love the overall soundscape. The production is clean and clear. At around 4:30, there are words spoken in what I believe is French. There are some really unique and cool sounds as they begin to bring the song to a close. I really liked that! There are some really different, unique tones, yet it is still accessible to most listeners. And if offering the listener something unique and different isn't progressive, I don't know what is!Track 2 - Chaos Dreaming (9:33)A spooky keyboard sound opens this one. At around 1:20, the rhythm section enters and creates a simple groove. The keyboards and guitar are now playing a melodic motif. About a minute later, the rhythm section temporarily drops out, and they begin a new theme. The vocals come in with the "enigmatic voice". After the 5-minute mark, we get an instrumental break. A reggae groove eventually emerges; I like it. Hansford Rowe has a nice bass tone on this. The vocals return afterwards. The chorus has a catchy hook on the title phrase. The effects that they use are captivating. Cool track, with a potentially ear-worm chorus.Track 3 - Siren Song (5:07)The opening sound effects do indeed invoke the siren's song. The vocals enter and lead the instruments in with a slow groove. This one is a little bit "doom-y". I like the vocal sound with lots of reverb and echoes. The contrast between the heavy doom-laden verses and the somewhat lighter choruses is nice. Good track, very engaging.Track 4 - Pool of Mirrors (5:54)Electric piano with a vibrating tone starts this one out. This one is a little bit lighter at a moderate tempo. The music sort of floats. This is not too far removed from something that 21 Pilots might do (and I am very much on the record that I believe that 21 Pilots are a modern art-rock band). There is even something of a rap at around 3:30. The rhythm section drops out around 4:30 and there is a quieter section. Eventually, the instruments drop off one by one, leaving the main keyboard riff and an acoustic guitar lead. The bass takes over from the guitar, then some wordless vocals bring the song to a close.Track 5 - Heaven's Rain (7:18)This one starts gently with sustained keyboard sounds, electric piano and acoustic guitar. Big tom-tom sounds punctuate the sound before and during the vocals. The "enigmatic voice" is very much in use here. There are some BIG accents just prior to the 2:30 mark. A cool groove keeps the track moving. I like the bass lines on this album. In fact, after 4:30, the bass is featured. I like this instrumental section. It is symphonic much like early King Crimson on "Epitaph". I believe I hear a mellotron. I truly appreciate the fact that even though this is an electronic music project by nature, there are still great dynamic shifts and some real guitars and basses in use. It brings in the human factor. Good track. Track 6 - Screaming Sound Machines (4:57)This begins with an orchestral fade in, then a beat emerges. This has a great groove. The lead vocals are in a low register. I like the feel of this one. At 2:25, there is a bit of a "breakdown" segment with a cool analog synth tone. There is a nice, but brief, guitar solo at around 3:30, presumably from Steve Bonino. This is a pretty cool track. I like the false ending before the final chord.Track 7 - Heavy Water (7:34)A quiet riff over a synth bed starts things off here. Some dissonant piano and sound effects join in. This one is feeling like a slow burn. More sounds enter as we go along. At around the 2-minute mark, the rhythm section makes a beat, and the vocals are downright creepy sounding. I like the refrain of the title with the lead vocals singing other words. Things get quiet for a moment in the middle of the song. The music gets big and powerful at around the 5-minute point. While the drum programming isn't bad, I'd love to hear this with a live drummer, as it's a little stiff sounding sometimes. The rest of the sounds are much more fluid (no pun intended). Track 8 - Inviolate Fields (9:51)The electric piano is the primary sound initially, but the soundscape grows. Guest vocalist Laura Piazzai's voice adds a new dimension to the sound. I already am familiar with her from her work on the Massimo Pieretti album I have reviewed on this blog (see the labels menu); she's wonderful. There is an awesome fretless bass feature at around the 3-minute mark. Quinn Blanchard's violin is kind of spooky in the way that Jimmy Page's bowed guitar is on Led Zeppelin's "In the Evening"; cool! There is a vibraphone tone that is sort of dominating the sound at around 5 minutes, that buries Laura's vocals in the mix, I wish she was brought out more. She comes out more as the song progresses. The overall feel is pretty laid-back on this longest track. I like the triangles or whatever the percussion sounds they are using are at around 8:30. The track just sort of winds down at the end. Piazzai's voice is the stand-out feature of this track. Track 9 - Are Friends Electric? (5:17)This is a cover of a Gary Numan song. A cool bass riff is the motif on this one. This one is moderately fast. The vocal melody is kind of catchy. There is a low-register spoken word section in the middle with a cool rhythmic backdrop. This one has a bit of an 80s new-wave vibe. There is another spoken-word section with about one minute remaining. They ride the riff out to the song's conclusion. OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:Electronic music isn't my biggest area of expertise, but I generally liked this album. The biggest drawback is the drum machine in my opinion. Hansford Rowe's bass playing is so strong and provides a real human element to the sound, but sometimes the drum machine fills were so stiff and mechanical that they didn't quite mesh. I understand that they are coming from a point of view of being "sound machines", so maybe that is what they are going for. From my perspective, however, adding a live drummer would improve their overall sound and be less distracting than the stiff drum machine is to me. There was a lot that I DO like about this album. There are some great riffs and soundscapes and musical concepts here. The vocal sounds, even the processed ones, are very engaging and interesting. Rowe's bass work is a real standout for me. Alain Bellaiche seems to be a good guitarist when he gets the spotlight. This album is really about the electronic sounds that the founding pair of Jeremie Arrobas and Thomas Szirmay bring to the table, however, and in that aspect, they have succeeded. The guest musicians, particularly Steve Bonino, Laura Piazzai, and Quinn Blanchard add a lot to the album. I'll give this an overall score of 4 out of 5 stars (80%), but fans of electronic music stylings will probably like it even more.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由蒙特利尔音乐人组合创作，属于跨界前卫摇滚范畴。整张作品以复古未来主义为美学方向，融合了合成器键盘、采样音效与吉他摇滚的质感。制作上注重声场构建，音色设计具有实验色彩——包括无品贝斯滑奏、迷幻键盘氛围、独特的效果器处理，以及法语念白段落。编曲在律动上展现出多样性，既有中速funk律动、雷鬼段落，也有氛围铺陈的段落过渡。主唱与"enigmatic voice"的人声交织形成层次感。专辑试图在前卫摇滚的框架内融入电子音效与多元节奏元素，在可听性与实验性之间寻求平衡，面向能够接受非主流声响但仍偏好旋律结构的听众。

items.body: Crucifera, the solo industrial project of New Jersey-based musician Danielle Astraea, released the single “Paint” on July 24, 2026. The track is self-released independently and available digitally on Bandcamp and other streaming platforms. It follows the debut album, “Exostential,” released April 3, 2026. “Paint” mixes industrial, trip-hop, gothic trap and witch-house elements. Astraea wrote, produced, recorded and mixed the track herself in her home studio, and Sebastian Komor (Icon of Coil, Xenomorph Productions) handled mastering, the same role he held on “Exostential.” The song is a dark, abrasive exploration of cognitive dissonance, attribution error and tribalistic projection, built around how people reduce other people to fixed caricatures – either idealized or demonized – rather than responding to who they actually are. Astraea describes her overall sound as “crunchy ethereal industrial music for spiders.” She works without a traditional drum kit, building the rhythm tracks from processed field and sound-design textures rather than sampled or programmed drum sounds, and composes each song first on acoustic piano and guitar before building out the electronic production in her home studio. Paint by crucifera About Crucifera Crucifera is the solo project of Danielle Astraea, a self-taught multi-instrumentalist, producer and visual artist based in New Jersey, United States. Astraea began her professional career in the arts and creative direction in 2000, but kept her original music private for years before releasing it under the Crucifera name. She writes, records, mixes and produces every Crucifera track herself, starting each composition on acoustic piano or nylon guitar before building the finished arrangement digitally in her home studio. Crucifera’s debut full-length album, “Exostential,” was released on April 3, 2026, preceded by the singles “saVior” and “Martyr Box.” The album was mastered by Sebastian Komor of Icon of Coil and Xenomorph Productions; “Martyr Box” was mixed by Steven Seibold of Hate Dept. Astraea has also contributed composition and remix work to other industrial acts outside her solo output. “Paint,” Crucifera’s first single since “Exostential,” continues the project’s fusion of acoustic songwriting roots and industrial electronic production, with Komor again handling mastering. A new Crucifera EP is planned for later in 2026, followed by a second full-length album in 2027.
items._cn_summary: Crucifera 是新泽西音乐人 Danielle Astraea 的个人工业项目，2026年7月发布单曲《Paint》，延续了首张专辑《Exostential》的方向。创作上她以原声钢琴与尼龙弦吉他为起点，在家庭工作室中铺设电子制作层，节奏部分不使用传统鼓组或采样鼓机，而是以处理过的田野录音和声音设计质感构建。她自述风格为"献给蜘蛛的脆响空灵工业音乐"，融合工业、trip-hop、哥特陷阱与巫屋元素。歌曲主题围绕认知失调与归因偏差展开，探讨人们如何将他人简化为固定漫画形象。母带由 Icon of Coil 成员 Sebastian Komor 处理，独立发行于 Bandcamp 等平台。整体制作手法具有个人特色，但文章为新闻发布性质，缺乏实际听感与音乐性深度评析。

It is the second single, after “Drill, Baby, Drill!”, from the band’s third album since their 2023 reunion, “Doom Pop!”, due September 4, 2026 via 9×9 Records on CD, digital and limited eco-vinyl, with North American distribution through Darla Records. “Things Have Learnt to Walk that Ought to Crawl” was originally written in 1982 and released that year as the band’s debut single for Red Flame Records. It is the only older song reworked for “Doom Pop!” and one of just three of the band’s 1980s songs that have remained in their live set. The new version was recorded and mixed at Ark Recording Studios in Liverpool by Steve Powell, produced by Dave Jackson and Steve Powell, and mastered by Pete Maher. “‘Things Have Learnt to Walk that Ought to Crawl’ is the only older song re-envisioned for this album, and one of only three 1980s songs by The Room to survive in our live set,” said Dave Jackson. “We decided to re-record and release it as it fits neatly into our new repertoire with its exhilarating jangly forward thrust, and also highlights Clive Thomas’ unique drumming.” On “Doom Pop!” as a whole, Jackson said: “We aimed at shorter, sharper, more pop-oriented songs than on our previous album ‘The Telling’, which was a continuous story told in eleven songs without repetition or distinct choruses. The ‘pop’ element mainly harks back to the roots of our music, updating our original spiky, post-punk independent sound with Ethan’s keyboard stylings. Lyrically, it is a response to the current climate of emerging fascism and paranoia that increasingly colonizes all media.” The current line-up features Dave Jackson (vocals), Becky Stringer (bass), Darren Brown (guitar), Ethan Kyme (keyboards, theremin) and original member Clive Thomas (drums), with Tom McCabe playing drums on two tracks. “Doom Pop!” follows “Restless Fate” (2023) and “The Telling” (2024), both also released via 9×9 Records. The Room’s live dates The Room play the following shows around the release of “Doom Pop!”: September 11, 2026 – Birkenhead, Future Yard September 12, 2026 – London, Aces & Eights September 26, 2026 – Liverpool, 81 Renshaw Street October 9, 2026 – Edinburgh, Wee Red Bar November 13, 2026 – London, Dublin Castle About The Room The Room formed in Liverpool in late 1979 around singer Dave Jackson, guitarist Robyn Odlum, bassist Becky Stringer and drummer Clive Thomas. Early releases on their own label, Box Records, drew comparisons in the press to Joy Division, The Fall and fellow Liverpool band Echo & The Bunnymen, and won the band support from John Peel, for whom they recorded four sessions, plus an appearance on “The Old Grey Whistle Test”. In 1982 the band signed to Red Flame Records, debuting with the single “Things Have Learnt to Walk that Ought to Crawl” and the album “Indoor Fireworks”. The line-up changed in 1983, with Odlum and Thomas replaced by drummer Alan Wills, guitarist Paul Cavanagh and keyboard player Peter Baker, a configuration that recorded the mini-album “Clear!”. Brass player Phil Lucking joined in 1984, ahead of the album “In Evil Hour”, part-produced by Television’s Tom Verlaine. The Room split in 1985; Jackson and Stringer went on to form Benny Profane, Dust and Dead Cowboys. The Room reunited in 2023, releasing the album “Restless Fate” via 9×9 Records that January, followed by the concept album “The Telling” in 2024. The current line-up of Jackson, Stringer, Darren Brown, Ethan Kyme and Clive Thomas, with Tom McCabe on drums for select tracks, now returns with “Doom Pop!”, due September 4, 2026, which includes the re-recorded “Things Have Learnt to Walk that Ought to Crawl” alongside new material.

items.body: Electronic duo Oui Plastique will release the single “Spirit” on September 4, 2026 through the Danish label Town and Towers Records, available on all digital platforms. It is the third single from the project’s upcoming second album, “Forever Will Be Over Before You Know It”, following “Revival” in April 2026 and “Linger” in June 2026. Oui Plastique consists of Martin Nyrup and James Thomas. “Spirit” is described as an atmospheric, slow-burning track that takes the listener to a dark place deep in the psyche, where the lines of reality blur. The B-side carries Oui Plastique’s own interpretation of John Barry’s theme for “The Persuaders”, the early-1970s TV series starring Roger Moore and Tony Curtis. Oui Plastique’s ‘Spirit’ and the album ‘Forever Will Be Over Before You Know It’ “Spirit” marks the duo’s continued run-up to “Forever Will Be Over Before You Know It”, their first full-length since 2022’s “Fraternity of Strangers”. No release date for the album has been confirmed beyond 2026. About Oui Plastique Oui Plastique grew out of a 2017 collaboration between Martin Nyrup, one half of the Danish-British dark wave duo Perpacity, and James Thomas of the band DVL, who together recorded the album “Convergence” that year. The Oui Plastique name followed, and in 2018 the pair recorded a three-track covers EP for the UnMute project, a tribute to Mute Records, released on Bandcamp as “UM EP 04” on February 1, 2019. The duo’s debut album “Fraternity of Strangers” was released on February 25, 2022 through ScentAir Records, as a limited CD and digital release containing eleven tracks. A remastered edition of “Convergence” followed in June 2022. In August 2025, the UnMute covers were remastered and reissued on all major platforms as the EP UnMute via Town and Towers Records. Oui Plastique previously released the singles “Revival” and Linger in April and June 2026 respectively, ahead of the second album. With “Spirit” set for September 4, 2026, Oui Plastique continue the build-up to “Forever Will Be Over Before You Know It”, their first full-length since their 2022 debut.
items._cn_summary: 丹麦-英国暗潮二人组 Oui Plastique 即将发布新单曲《Spirit》，这是他们第二张专辑《Forever Will Be Over Before You Know It》的第三支先行曲，由丹麦小厂牌 Town and Towers Records 发行的数字单曲。作品被描述为氛围感浓郁、缓慢燃烧的曲目，将听众带入心理深处的黑暗地带，现实与虚幻的边界在此模糊。值得一提的是 B 面收录了二人对 John Barry 七零年代电视剧《The Persuaders!》主题曲的重新诠释，展现了老牌影视配乐与暗潮电子语汇之间的对话可能。乐队成员 Martin Nyrup 与 James Thomas 此前各自在 Perpacity 和 DVL 等项目中积累了暗潮创作经验。整体而言，这是一篇以信息发布为主的新闻稿，对音乐本身的分析性评论较为有限。
